Not "perfect men"; for the many members constitute but one Church joined to the one Christ.<div eID="gen35608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35609" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stature, &c.--</hi>The standard of spiritual "stature" is "the fulness of Christ," that is, which Christ has (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.23">Ep 1:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.19">3:19</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Gal.4.19">Ga 4:19</reference>); that the body should be worthy of the Head, the perfect Christ. <div eID="gen35609" type="x-p"/>
entries.1eafeffaf6cd11fa5e824f4ebf2fc9fb1f8e3c9c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17648"/><div sID="gen35610" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17648"/>14. Translate, "To the end that"; the aim of the bestowal of gifts stated negatively, as in <reference osisRef="Eph.4.13">Ep 4:13</reference> it is stated positively.<div eID="gen35610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35611" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tossed to and fro--</hi>inwardly, even without wind; like billows of the sea. So the Greek. Compare <reference osisRef="Jas.1.6">Jas 1:6</reference>.<div eID="gen35611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35612" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">carried about--</hi>with every wind from without.<div eID="gen35612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35613" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">doctrine--</hi>"teaching." The various teachings are the "winds" which keep them tossed on a sea of doubts (<reference osisRef="Heb.13.9">He 13:9</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Matt.11.7">Mt 11:7</reference>).<div eID="gen35613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35614" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by--</hi>Greek, "in"; expressing "the evil atmosphere in which the varying currents of doctrine exert their force" [Ellicott].<div eID="gen35614" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35615" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sleight--</hi>literally, "dice playing." The player frames his throws of the dice so that the numbers may turn up which best suit his purpose.<div eID="gen35615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35616" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of men--</hi>contrasted with Christ (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.13">Ep 4:13</reference>).<div eID="gen35616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35617" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and--</hi>Greek, "in."<div eID="gen35617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35618" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cunning craftiness, whereby they lie in wait to deceive--</hi>Translate as Greek, "craftiness tending to the methodized system of deceit" ("the schemes of error") [Alford]. Bengel takes "deceit," or "error," to stand for "the parent of error," Satan (compare <reference osisRef="Eph.6.11">Ep 6:11</reference>); referring to his concealed mode of acting. <div eID="gen35618" type="x-p"/>
entries.a3c7f22915a23a50d5e7c8fd7c1a610482b75d93: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17649"/><div sID="gen35619" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17649"/><hi type="bold">15. speaking the truth--</hi>Translate, "holding the truth"; "following the truth"; opposed to "error" or "deceit" (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.14">Ep 4:14</reference>).<div eID="gen35619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35620" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in love--</hi>"Truth" is never to be sacrificed to so-called "charity"; yet it is to be maintained in charity. Truth in word and act, love in manner and spirit, are the Christian's rule (compare <reference osisRef="Eph.4.21">Ep 4:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.4.24">24</reference>).<div eID="gen35620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35621" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">grow up--</hi>from the state of "children" to that of "full-grown men." There is growth only in the spiritually alive, not in the dead.<div eID="gen35621" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35622" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">into him--</hi>so as to be more and more incorporated with Him, and become one with Him.<div eID="gen35622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35623" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the head--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Eph.1.22">Ep 1:22</reference>). <div eID="gen35623" type="x-p"/>
entries.590db90aafc19e4a10a6219ffa7a6cd636051772: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17650"/><div sID="gen35624" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17650"/>16. (<reference osisRef="Col.2.19">Col 2:19</reference>).<div eID="gen35624" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35625" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fitly joined together--</hi>"being fitly framed together," as in <reference osisRef="Eph.2.21">Ep 2:21</reference>; all the parts being in their proper position, and in mutual relation.<div eID="gen35625" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35626" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">compacted--</hi>implying firm consolidation.<div eID="gen35626" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35627" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by that which every joint supplieth--</hi>Greek, "by means of every joint of the supply"; joined with "maketh increase of the body," not with "compacted." "By every ministering (supplying) joint." The joints are the points of union where the supply passes to the different members, furnishing the body with the materials of its growth.<div eID="gen35627" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35628" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">effectual working--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Eph.1.19">Ep 1:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.7">3:7</reference>). According to the effectual working of grace in each member (or else, rather, "according to each several member's working"), proportioned to the measure of its need of supply.<div eID="gen35628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35629" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">every part--</hi>Greek, "each one part"; each individual part.<div eID="gen35629" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35630" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">maketh increase--</hi>Translate, as the Greek is the same as <reference osisRef="Eph.4.15">Ep 4:15</reference>, "maketh (carrieth on) the growth of the body." <div eID="gen35630" type="x-p"/>
entries.8782a2ac1367b82921d5cf7f95a649380dbbc126: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17651"/><div sID="gen35631" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17651"/><hi type="bold">17. therefore--</hi>resuming the exhortation which he had begun with, "I therefore beseech you that ye walk worthy," &c. (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.1">Ep 4:1</reference>).<div eID="gen35631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35632" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">testify in the Lord--</hi>in whom (as our element) we do all things pertaining to the ministry (<reference osisRef="1Thess.4.1">1Th 4:1</reference> [Alford]; <reference osisRef="Rom.9.1">Ro 9:1</reference>).<div eID="gen35632" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35633" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">henceforth ... not--</hi>Greek, "no longer"; resumed from <reference osisRef="Eph.4.14">Ep 4:14</reference>.<div eID="gen35633" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35634" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">other--</hi>Greek, "the rest of the Gentiles."<div eID="gen35634" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35635" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the vanity, &c.--</hi>as their element: opposed to "in the Lord." "Vanity of mind" is the waste of the rational powers on worthless objects, of which idolatry is one of the more glaring instances. The root of it is departure from the knowledge of the true God (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.18">Ep 4:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.4.19">19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.1.21">Ro 1:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.5">1Th 4:5</reference>). <div eID="gen35635" type="x-p"/>
entries.02cdcdcc5e52ba6a88a14446de18be4186ae561a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17652"/><div sID="gen35636" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17652"/>18. More literally, "Being darkened in their understanding," that is, their intelligence, or perceptions (compare <reference osisRef="Eph.5.8">Ep 5:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.26.18">Ac 26:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.4">1Th 5:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.5">5</reference>).<div eID="gen35636" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35637" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">alienated--</hi>This and "darkened," imply that before the fall they (in the person of their first father) had been partakers of life and light: and that they had revolted from the primitive revelation (compare <reference osisRef="Eph.2.12">Ep 2:12</reference>).<div eID="gen35637" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35638" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">life of God--</hi>that life whereby God lives in His own people: as He was the life and light in Adam before the irruption of death and darkness into human nature; and as He is the life in the regenerate (<reference osisRef="Gal.2.20">Ga 2:20</reference>). "Spiritual life in believers is kindled from the life itself of God" [Bengel].<div eID="gen35638" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35639" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">through--</hi>rather as Greek, "on account of the ignorance," namely, of God. Wilful ignorance in the first instance, their fathers not "choosing to retain God in their knowledge." This is the beginning point of their misery (<reference osisRef="Acts.17.30">Ac 17:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.1.21">Ro 1:21</reference>, 23, 28; <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.14">1Pe 1:14</reference>).<div eID="gen35639" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35640" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">because of--</hi>"on account of."<div eID="gen35640" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35641" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">blindness--</hi>Greek, "hardness," literally, the hardening of the skin so as not to be sensible of touch. Hence a soul's callousness to feeling (<reference osisRef="Mark.3.5">Mr 3:5</reference>). Where there is spiritual "life" ("the life of God") there is feeling; where there is not, there is "hardness." <div eID="gen35641" type="x-p"/>
entries.4c2950510302c5f482b72e236ffa4227667542e0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17653"/><div sID="gen35642" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17653"/><hi type="bold">19. past feeling--</hi>senseless, shameless, hopeless; the ultimate result of a long process of "hardening," or habit of sin (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.18">Ep 4:18</reference>). "Being past hope," or despairing, is the reading of the Vulgate; though not so well supported as English Version reading, "past feeling," which includes the absence of hope (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.25">Jr 2:25</reference>; 18:12).<div eID="gen35642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35643" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">given themselves over--</hi>In <reference osisRef="Rom.1.24">Ro 1:24</reference> it is, "God gave them up to uncleanness." Their giving themselves to it was punished in kind, God giving them up to it by withdrawing His preventing grace; their sin thus was made their punishment. They gave themselves up of their own accord to the slavery of their lust, to do all its pleasure, as captives who have ceased to strive with the foe. God gave them up to it, but not against their will; for they give themselves up to it [Zanchius].<div eID="gen35643" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35644" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lasciviousness--</hi>"wantonness" [Alford]. So it is translated in <reference osisRef="Rom.13.13">Ro 13:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.18">2Pe 2:18</reference>. It does not necessarily include lasciviousness; but it means intemperate, reckless readiness for it, and for every self-indulgence. "The first beginnings of unchastity" [Grotius]. "Lawless insolence, and wanton caprice" [Trench].<div eID="gen35644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35645" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to work all uncleanness--</hi>The Greek implies, "with a deliberate view to the working (as if it were their work or business, not a mere accidental fall into sin) of uncleanness of every kind."<div eID="gen35645" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35646" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with greediness--</hi>Greek, "in greediness." Uncleanness and greediness of gain often go hand in hand (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.3">Ep 5:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.5.5">5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.3.5">Col 3:5</reference>); though "greediness" here includes all kinds of self-seeking. <div eID="gen35646" type="x-p"/>
entries.5ffad4df01349d57bdb9a65b7cc8d7d01c9c2499: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17654"/><div sID="gen35647" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17654"/><hi type="bold">20. learned Christ--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Phil.3.10">Php 3:10</reference>). To know Christ Himself, is the great lesson of the Christian life: this the Ephesians began to learn at their conversion. "Christ," in reference to His office, is here specified as the object of learning. "Jesus," in <reference osisRef="Eph.4.21">Ep 4:21</reference>, as the person. <div eID="gen35647" type="x-p"/>
entries.def12ed7c44aaa5f96076f00001eb135b698470a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17655"/><div sID="gen35648" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17655"/><hi type="bold">21. If so be that--</hi>not implying doubt; assuming what I have no reason to doubt, that<div eID="gen35648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35649" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">heard him--</hi>The "Him" is emphatic: "heard Himself," not merely heard about Him.<div eID="gen35649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35650" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">taught by him--</hi>Greek, "taught IN Him," that is, being in vital union with Him (<reference osisRef="Rom.16.7">Ro 16:7</reference>).<div eID="gen35650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35651" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as the truth is in Jesus--</hi>Translate in connection with "taught"; "And in Him have been taught, according as is truth in Jesus." There is no article in the Greek. "Truth" is therefore used in the most comprehensive sense, truth in its essence, and highest perfection, in Jesus; "if according as it is thus in Him, ye have been so taught in Him"; in contrast to "the vanity of mind of the Gentiles" (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.17">Ep 4:17</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="John.1.14">Joh 1:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.17">17</reference>; 18:37). Contrast <reference osisRef="John.8.44">Joh 8:44</reference>. <div eID="gen35651" type="x-p"/>
entries.9afa3a160cbbf71f3f2288ecccc49eb520c22f78: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17656"/><div sID="gen35652" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17656"/><hi type="bold">22. That ye--</hi>following "Ye have been taught" (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.21">Ep 4:21</reference>).<div eID="gen35652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35653" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">concerning the former conversation--</hi>"in respect to your former way of life."<div eID="gen35653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35654" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the old man--</hi>your old unconverted nature (<reference osisRef="Rom.6.6">Ro 6:6</reference>).<div eID="gen35654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35655" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">is corrupt according to the deceitful lusts--</hi>rather, "which is being corrupted ('perisheth,' compare <reference osisRef="Gal.6.8">Ga 6:8</reference>, 'corruption,' that is, destruction) according to (that is, as might be expected from) the lusts of deceit." Deceit is personified; lusts are its servants and tools. In contrast to "the holiness of the truth," <reference osisRef="Eph.4.24">Ep 4:24</reference>, and "truth in Jesus," <reference osisRef="Eph.4.21">Ep 4:21</reference>; and answering to Gentile "vanity," <reference osisRef="Eph.4.17">Ep 4:17</reference>. Corruption and destruction are inseparably associated together. The man's old-nature-lusts are his own executioners, fitting him more and more for eternal corruption and death. <div eID="gen35655" type="x-p"/>
entries.5746b8d65c9afe90e1c774677cae9db89d7ee8c6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17657"/><div sID="gen35656" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17657"/><hi type="bold">23. be renewed--</hi>The Greek (ananeousthai) implies "the continued renewal in the youth of the new man." A different Greek word (anakainousthai) implies "renewal from the old state."<div eID="gen35656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35657" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the spirit of your mind--</hi>As there is no Greek for "in," which there is at <reference osisRef="Eph.4.17">Ep 4:17</reference>, "in the vanity of their mind," it is better to translate, "By the Spirit of your mind," that is, by your new spiritual nature; the restored and divinely informed leading principle of the mind. The "spirit" of man in New Testament is only then used in its proper sense, as worthy of its place and governing functions, when it is one spirit with the Lord. The natural, or animal man, is described as "not having the Spirit" (Jude 19) [Alford]. Spirit is not in this sense attributed to the unregenerate (<reference osisRef="1Thess.5.23">1Th 5:23</reference>). <div eID="gen35657" type="x-p"/>
entries.bafcba1cb632e7a00ccae43874d64f9f2477d93a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17658"/><div sID="gen35658" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17658"/><hi type="bold">24. put on the new man--</hi>Opposed to "the old man," which is to be "put off" (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.22">Ep 4:22</reference>). The Greek here (kainon) is different from that for "re-new-ed" (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.23">Ep 4:23</reference>). Put on not merely a renovated nature, but a new, that is, altogether different nature, a changed nature (compare Note,, see on <reference osisRef="Col.3.10">Col 3:10</reference>).<div eID="gen35658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35659" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">after God, &c.--</hi>Translate, "Which hath been created (once for all: so the Greek aorist means: in Christ, <reference osisRef="Eph.2.10">Ep 2:10</reference>; so that in each believer it has not to be created again, but to be put on) after (the image of) God" (<reference osisRef="Gen.1.27">Ge 1:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.3.10">Col 3:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.15">1Pe 1:15</reference>), &c. God's image in which the first Adam was originally created, is restored, to us far more gloriously in the second Adam, the image of the invisible God (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.4">2Co 4:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.1.15">Col 1:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.1.3">He 1:3</reference>).<div eID="gen35659" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35660" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in righteousness--</hi>"IN" it as the element of the renewed man.<div eID="gen35660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35661" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">true holiness--</hi>rather, as the Greek, "holiness of the truth"; holiness flowing from sincere following of "the truth of God" (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.25">Ro 1:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.7">3:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.8">15:8</reference>): opposed to "the lusts of deceit" (Greek, <reference osisRef="Eph.4.22">Ep 4:22</reference>); compare also <reference osisRef="Eph.4.21">Ep 4:21</reference>, "truth is in Jesus." "Righteousness" is in relation to our fellow men, the second table of the law; "Holiness," in relation to God, the first table; the religious observance of offices of piety (compare <reference osisRef="Luke.1.75">Lu 1:75</reference>). In the parallel (<reference osisRef="Col.3.10">Col 3:10</reference>) it is, "renewed in knowledge after the image," &c. As at Colosse the danger was from false pretenders to knowledge, the true "knowledge" which flows from renewal of the heart is dwelt on; so at Ephesus, the danger being from the corrupt morals prevalent around, the renewal in "holiness," contrasted with the Gentile "uncleanness" (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.19">Ep 4:19</reference>), and "righteousness," in contrast to "greediness," is made prominent. <div eID="gen35661" type="x-p"/>
entries.7b248e618911aeb641d5862695c7a174dea50c2c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17659"/><div sID="gen35662" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17659"/><hi type="bold">25. Wherefore--</hi>From the general character of "the new man," there will necessarily result the particular features which he now details.<div eID="gen35662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35663" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">putting away--</hi>Greek, "having put away" once for all.<div eID="gen35663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35664" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lying--</hi>"falsehood": the abstract. "Speak ye truth each one with his neighbor," is quoted, slightly changed, from <reference osisRef="Zech.8.16">Zec 8:16</reference>. For "to," Paul quotes it "with," to mark our inner connection with one another, as "members one of another" [Stier]. Not merely members of one body. Union to one another in Christ, not merely the external command, instinctively leads Christians to fulfil mutual duties. One member could not injure or deceive another, without injuring himself, as all have a mutual and common interest. <div eID="gen35664" type="x-p"/>
entries.3fbf7ad55426c96cf309cba27ba1d4ead50e8f00: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17660"/><div sID="gen35665" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17660"/><hi type="bold">26. Be ye angry, and sin not--</hi>So the Septuagint, <reference osisRef="Ps.4.4">Psa 4:4</reference>. Should circumstances arise to call for anger on your part, let it be as Christ's "anger" (<reference osisRef="Mark.3.5">Mr 3:5</reference>), without sin. Our natural feelings are not wrong when directed to their legitimate object, and when not exceeding due bounds. As in the future literal, so in the present spiritual, resurrection, no essential constituent is annihilated, but all that is a perversion of the original design is removed. Thus indignation at dishonor done to God, and wrong to man, is justifiable anger. Passion is sinful (derived from "passio," suffering: implying that amidst seeming energy, a man is really passive, the slave of his anger, instead of ruling it).<div eID="gen35665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35666" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">let not the sun go down upon your wrath--</hi>"wrath" is absolutely forbidden; "anger" not so, though, like poison sometimes used as medicine, it is to be used with extreme caution. The sense is not, Your anger shall not be imputed to you if you put it away before nightfall; but "let no wrath (that is, as the Greek, personal 'irritation' or 'exasperation') mingle with your 'anger,' even though, the latter be righteous, [Trench, Greek Synonyms of the New Testament]. "Put it away before sunset" (when the Jewish day began), is proverbial for put it away at once before another day begin (<reference osisRef="Deut.24.15">De 24:15</reference>); also before you part with your brother for the night, perhaps never in this world to meet again. So Jona, "Let not night and anger against anyone sleep with you, but go and conciliate the other party, though he have been the first to commit the offense." Let not your "anger" at another's wickedness verge into hatred, or contempt, or revenge [Vatablus]. <div eID="gen35666" type="x-p"/>
entries.48e62d5353b1558a350573c826ec460a3852690f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17661"/><div sID="gen35667" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17661"/><hi type="bold">27. Neither give place--</hi>that is, occasion, or scope, to the devil, by continuing in "wrath." The keeping of anger through the darkness of night, is giving place to the devil, the prince of darkness (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.12">Ep 6:12</reference>). <div eID="gen35667" type="x-p"/>
entries.fcd91c5a6e0d3bda2cfd29349c4715bd72e1dda9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17662"/><div sID="gen35668" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17662"/>28. Greek, "Let him that stealeth." The imperfect or past tense is, however, mainly meant, though not to the exclusion of the present. "Let the stealing person steal no more." Bandits frequented the mountains near Ephesus. Such are meant by those called "thieves" in the New Testament.<div eID="gen35668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35669" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but rather--</hi>For it is not enough to cease from a sin, but the sinner must also enter on the path that is its very opposite [Chrysostom]. The thief, when repentant, should labor more than he would be called on to do, if he had never stolen.<div eID="gen35669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35670" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">let him labour--</hi>Theft and idleness go together.<div eID="gen35670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35671" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the thing which is good--</hi>in contrast with theft, the thing which was evil in his past character.<div eID="gen35671" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35672" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with his hands--</hi>in contrast with his former thievish use of his hands.<div eID="gen35672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35673" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that he may have to give--</hi>"that he may have wherewith to impart." He who has stolen should exercise liberality beyond the restitution of what he has taken. Christians in general should make not selfish gain their aim in honest industry, but the acquisition of the means of greater usefulness to their fellow men; and the being independent of the alms of others. So Paul himself (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.35">Ac 20:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Thess.3.8">2Th 3:8</reference>) acted as he taught (<reference osisRef="1Thess.4.11">1Th 4:11</reference>). <div eID="gen35673" type="x-p"/>
entries.5c4ec173d36576fd782efcf0c64220889925bede: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17663"/><div sID="gen35674" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17663"/><hi type="bold">29. corrupt--</hi>literally, "insipid," without "the salt of grace" (<reference osisRef="Col.4.6">Col 4:6</reference>), so worthless and then becoming corrupt: included in "foolish talking" (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.4">Ep 5:4</reference>). Its opposite is "that which is good to edifying."<div eID="gen35674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35675" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">communication--</hi>language.<div eID="gen35675" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35676" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that which, &c.--</hi>Greek, "whatever is good."<div eID="gen35676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35677" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">use of edifying--</hi>literally, "for edifying of the need," that is, for edifying where it is needed. Seasonably edifying; according as the occasion and present needs of the hearers require, now censure, at another time consolation. Even words good in themselves must be introduced seasonably lest by our fault they prove injurious instead of useful. Trench explains, Not vague generalities, which would suit a thousand other cases equally well, and probably equally ill: our words should be as nails fastened in a sure place, words suiting the present time and the present person, being "for the edifying of the occasion" (<reference osisRef="Col.4.6">Col 4:6</reference>).<div eID="gen35677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35678" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">minister--</hi>Greek, "give." The word spoken "gives grace to the hearers" when God uses it as His instrument for that purpose. <div eID="gen35678" type="x-p"/>
entries.90d25540425b4faa3f3cca44eb9a0f1a33bdbaee: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17664"/><div sID="gen35679" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17664"/><hi type="bold">30. grieve not--</hi>A condescension to human modes of thought most touching. Compare "vexed His Holy Spirit" (<reference osisRef="Isa.63.10">Is 63:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.78.40">Psa 78:40</reference>); "fretted me" (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.43">Eze 16:43</reference>: implying His tender love to us); and of hardened unbelievers, "resist the Holy Ghost" (<reference osisRef="Acts.7.51">Ac 7:51</reference>). This verse refers to believers, who grieve the Spirit by inconsistencies such as in the context are spoken of, corrupt or worthless conversation, &c.<div eID="gen35679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35680" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">whereby ye are sealed--</hi>rather, "wherein (or 'in whom') ye were sealed." As in <reference osisRef="Eph.1.13">Ep 1:13</reference>, believers are said to be sealed "in" Christ, so here "in the Holy Spirit," who is one with Christ, and who reveals Christ in the soul: the Greek implies that the sealing was done already once for all. It is the Father "BY" whom believers, as well as the Son Himself, were sealed (<reference osisRef="John.6.27">Joh 6:27</reference>). The Spirit is represented as itself the seal (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.13">Ep 1:13</reference>, for the image employed, see on <reference osisRef="Eph.1.13">Ep 1:13</reference>). Here the Spirit is the element IN which the believer is sealed, His gracious influences being the seal itself.<div eID="gen35680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35681" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto--</hi>kept safely against the day of redemption, namely, of the completion of redemption in the deliverance of the body as well as the soul from all sin and sorrow (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.14">Ep 1:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.21.28">Lu 21:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.8.23">Ro 8:23</reference>). <div eID="gen35681" type="x-p"/>
entries.722ed6807ad750e1d30d32a4450d342e7579c3b9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17665"/><div sID="gen35682" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17665"/><hi type="bold">31. bitterness--</hi>both of spirit and of speech: opposed to "kind."<div eID="gen35682" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35683" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wrath--</hi>passion for a time: opposed to "tender-hearted." Whence Bengel translates for "wrath," harshness.<div eID="gen35683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35684" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">anger--</hi>lasting resentment: opposed to "forgiving one another."<div eID="gen35684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35685" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">clamour--</hi>compared by Chrysostom to a horse carrying anger for its rider: "Bridle the horse, and you dismount its rider." "Bitterness" begets "wrath"; "wrath," "anger"; "anger," "clamor"; and "clamor," the more chronic "evil-speaking," slander, insinuations, and surmises of evil. "Malice" is the secret root of all: "fires fed within, and not appearing to by-standers from without, are the most formidable" [Chrysostom]. <div eID="gen35685" type="x-p"/>
entries.7444552d6b66d3b860ed21e1909c35e0bc5a844f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17666"/><div sID="gen35686" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17666"/>32. (<reference osisRef="Luke.7.42">Lu 7:42</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.3.12">Col 3:12</reference>).<div eID="gen35686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35687" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">even as--</hi>God hath shown Himself "kind, tender-hearted, and forgiving to you"; it is but just that you in turn shall be so to your fellow men, who have not erred against you in the degree that you have erred against God (<reference osisRef="Matt.18.33">Mt 18:33</reference>).<div eID="gen35687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35688" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">God for Christ's sake--</hi>rather as Greek, "God in Christ" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.19">2Co 5:19</reference>). It is in Christ that God vouchsafes forgiveness to us. It cost God the death of His Son, as man, to forgive us. It costs us nothing to forgive our fellow man.<div eID="gen35688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35689" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hath forgiven--</hi>rather as Greek, "forgave you." God has, once for all, forgiven sin in Christ, as a past historical fact. <chapter eID="Eph.4"/>

entries.9cfd4d406a97a435cde62d650302e8bee6fe9303: <div eID="gen50143" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen50144" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen50145" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen50145" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen50144" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen50146" type="x-p"/> The apostle exhorts them to walk worthy of their vocation, and to live in peace and unity, <reference osisRef="Eph.4.1-Eph.4.6">Eph 4:1-6</reference>. Shows that God has distributed a variety of gifts, and instituted a variety of offices in his Church, for the building up and perfecting of the body of Christ, <reference osisRef="Eph.4.7-Eph.4.13">Eph 4:7-13</reference>. Teaches them the necessity of being well instructed and steady in Divine things, <reference osisRef="Eph.4.14">Eph 4:14</reference>. Teaches how the body or Church of Christ is constituted, <reference osisRef="Eph.4.15">Eph 4:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.4.16">Eph 4:16</reference>. Warns them against acting like the Gentiles, of whose conduct he gives a lamentable description, <reference osisRef="Eph.4.17-Eph.4.19">Eph 4:17-19</reference>. Points out how they had been changed, in consequence of their conversion to Christianity, <reference osisRef="Eph.4.20">Eph 4:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.4.21">Eph 4:21</reference>. Gives various exhortations relative to the purification of their minds, their conduct to each other, and to the poor, <reference osisRef="Eph.4.22-Eph.4.28">Eph 4:22-28</reference>. Shows them that their conversation should be chaste and holy, that they might not grieve the Spirit of God; that they should avoid all bad tempers, be kindly affectioned one to another, and be of a forgiving spirit, <reference osisRef="Eph.4.29-Eph.4.32">Eph 4:29-32</reference>. <div eID="gen50146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50147" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen50147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50148" type="x-p"/> I therefore - Therefore, because God has provided for you such an abundant salvation, and ye have his testimonies among you, and have full liberty to use all the means of grace; <div eID="gen50148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50149" type="x-p"/> The prisoner of the Lord - Who am deprived of my liberty for the Lord's sake. <div eID="gen50149" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50150" type="x-p"/> Beseech you that ye walk - Ye have your liberty, and may walk; I am deprived of mine, and cannot. This is a fine stroke, and wrought up into a strong argument. You who are at large can show forth the virtues of him who called you into his marvellous light; I am in bondage, and can only exhort others by my writing, and show my submission to God by my patient suffering. <div eID="gen50150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50151" type="x-p"/> The vocation wherewith ye are called - The calling, κλησις, is the free invitation they have had from God to receive the privileges of the Gospel, and become his sons and daughters, without being obliged to observe Jewish rites and ceremonies. Their vocation, or calling, took in their Christian profession, with all the doctrines, precepts, privileges, duties, etc., of the Christian religion. <div eID="gen50151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50152" type="x-p"/> Among us, a man's calling signifies his trade, or occupation in life; that at which he works, and by which he gets his bread; and it is termed his calling, because it is supposed that God, in the course of his providence, calls the person to be thus employed, and thus to acquire his livelihood. Now, as it is a very poor calling by which a man cannot live, so it is a poor religion by which a man cannot get his soul saved. If, however, a man have an honest and useful trade, and employ himself diligently in labouring at it, he will surely be able to maintain himself by it; but without care, attention, and industry, he is not likely to get, even by this providential calling, the necessaries of life. In like manner, if a man do not walk worthy of his heavenly calling, i.e. suitable to its prescriptions, spirit, and design, he is not likely to get his soul saved unto eternal life. The best trade, unpractised, will not support any man; the most pure and holy religion of the Lord Jesus, unapplied, will save no soul. Many suppose, because they have a sound faith, that all is safe and well: as well might the mechanic, who knows he has a good trade, and that he understands the principles of it well, suppose it will maintain him, though he brings none of its principles into action by honest, assiduous, and well-directed labor. <div eID="gen50152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50153" type="x-p"/> Some suppose that the calling refers to the epithets usually given to the Christians; such as children of Abraham, children of God, true Israel of God, heirs of God, saints, fellow citizens with the saints, etc., etc.; and that these honorable appellations must be a strong excitement to the Ephesians to walk worthy of these exalted characters But I do not find that the word κλησις, calling, is taken in this sense any where in the New Testament; but that it has the meaning which I have given it above is evident from <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.20">1Cor 7:20</reference> : Εκαστος εν τη κλησει ᾑ εκληθη, εν ταυτῃ μενετω· Let every man abide in the calling to which he hath been called. The context shows that condition, employment, or business of life, is that to which the apostle refers.
entries.2f6925746653bf55117fb1653643d65f0f7a8a89: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen50153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50154" type="x-p"/> With all lowliness - It is by acting as the apostle here directs that a man walks worthy of this high vocation; ταπεινοφροσυνη signifies subjection or humility of mind. <div eID="gen50154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50155" type="x-p"/> Meekness - The opposite to anger and irritability of disposition. <div eID="gen50155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50156" type="x-p"/> Long-suffering - Μακροθυμια· Long-mindedness - never permitting a trial or provocation to get to the end of your patience. <div eID="gen50156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50157" type="x-p"/> Forbearing one another - Ανεχομενοι αλληλων· Sustaining one another - helping to support each other in all the miseries and trials of life: or, if the word be taken in the sense of bearing with each other, it may mean that, through the love of God working in our hearts, we should bear with each other's infirmities, ignorance, etc., knowing how much others have been or are still obliged to bear with us.
entries.6e32317084599974474ba9b03690edbc336a1d14: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen50157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50158" type="x-p"/> Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace - There can be no doubt that the Church at Ephesus was composed partly of converted Jews, as well as Gentiles. Now, from the different manner in which they had been brought up, there might be frequent causes of altercation. Indeed, the Jews, though converted, might be envious that the Gentiles were admitted to the same glorious privileges with themselves, without being initiated into them by bearing the yoke and burden of the Mosaic law. The apostle guards them against this, and shows them that they should intensely labor (for so the word σπουδαζειν implies) to promote and preserve peace and unity. By the unity of the Spirit we are to understand, not only a spiritual unity, but also a unity of sentiments, desires, and affections, such as is worthy of and springs from the Spirit of God. By the bond of peace we are to understand a peace or union, where the interests of all parties are concentrated, cemented, and sealed; the Spirit of God being the seal upon this knot.
entries.0795302a103da1d68c9c8f52e9363df60f47ea2e: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen50158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50159" type="x-p"/> There is one body - Viz. of Christ, which is his Church. <div eID="gen50159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50160" type="x-p"/> One Spirit - The Holy Ghost, who animates this body. <div eID="gen50160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50161" type="x-p"/> One hope - Of everlasting glory, to which glory ye have been called by the preaching of the Gospel; through which ye have become the body of Christ, instinct with the energy of the Holy Ghost.
entries.9fa4b41c77ab8182a294a80eeabef51bbc152a95: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen50161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50162" type="x-p"/> One Lord - Jesus Christ, who is the governor of this Church. <div eID="gen50162" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50163" type="x-p"/> One faith - One system of religion, proposing the same objects to the faith of all. <div eID="gen50163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50164" type="x-p"/> One baptism - Administered in the name of the holy Trinity; indicative of the influences, privileges, and effects of the Christian religion.
entries.deac339374861af58a40858d8d3f934518bda730: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen50164" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50165" type="x-p"/> One God - The fountain of all being, self-existent and eternal; and Father of all, both Jews and Gentiles, because he is the Father of the spirits of all flesh. <div eID="gen50165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50166" type="x-p"/> Who is above all - Ὁ επι παντων· Who is over all; as the King of kings, and Lord of lords. <div eID="gen50166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50167" type="x-p"/> And through all - Pervading every thing; being present with every thing; providing for all creatures; and by his energy supporting all things. <div eID="gen50167" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50168" type="x-p"/> And in you all - By the energy of his Spirit, enlightening, quickening, purifying, and comforting; in a word, making your hearts the temples of the Holy Ghost. Some think the mystery of the blessed Trinity is contained in this verse: God is over all, as Father; through all, by the Logos or Word; and in all, by the Holy Spirit.
entries.f350ac542ee508b436d1556e587bbe1b61b6d062: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen50168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50169" type="x-p"/> Unto every one of us is given grace - Grace may here signify a particular office; as if the apostle had said: Though we are all equal in the respects already mentioned, yet we have all different offices and situations to fill up in the Church and in the world; and we receive a free gift from Christ, according to the nature of the office, that we may be able to discharge it according to his own mind. So the free gift, which we receive from Christ, is according to the office or function which he has given us to fulfill; and the office is according to that free gift, each suited to the other.
entries.dc6a601b82b9b3c7ee934a660f813ec200664d51: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen50169" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50170" type="x-p"/> Wherefore he saith - The reference seems to be to <reference osisRef="Psa.68.18">Psa 68:18</reference>, which, however it may speak of the removal of the tabernacle, appears to have been intended to point out the glorious ascension of Christ after his resurrection from the dead. The expositions of various commentators have made the place extremely difficult. I shall not trouble my reader with them; they may be seen in Rosenmuller. <div eID="gen50170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50171" type="x-p"/> When he ascended up on high - The whole of this verse, as it stands in the psalm, seems to refer to a military triumph. Take the following paraphrase: Thou hast ascended on high: the conqueror was placed in a very elevated chariot. Thou hast led captivity captive: the conquered kings and generals were usually bound behind the chariot of the conqueror, to grace the triumph. Thou host received gifts for (Paul, given gifts unto) men: at such times the conqueror was wont to throw money among the crowd. Even to the rebellious: those who had fought against him now submit unto him, and share his munificence; for it is the property of a hero to be generous. That the Lord God might dwell among them: the conqueror being now come to fix his abode in the conquered provinces, and subdue the people to his laws. <div eID="gen50171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50172" type="x-p"/> All this the apostle applies to the resurrection, ascension, and glory of Christ; though it has been doubted by some learned men whether the psalmist had this in view. I shall not dispute about this; it is enough for me that the apostle, under the inspiration of God, applied the verse in this way; and whatever David might intend, and of whatever event he might have written, we see plainly that the sense in which the apostle uses it was the sense of the Spirit of God; for the Spirit in the Old and New Testaments is the same. I may venture a short criticism on a few words in the original: Thou hast received gifts for men, לקחת מתנות באדם lakachta mattanoth baadam, thou hast taken gifts in man, in Adam. The gifts which Jesus Christ distributes to man he has received in man, in and by virtue of his incarnation; and it is in consequence of his being made man that it may be said, The Lord God dwells among them; for Jesus was called Immanuel, God with us, in consequence of his incarnation. This view of the subject is consistent with the whole economy of grace, and suits well with the apostle's application of the words of the psalmist in this place.
entries.70251c5dd5e1c2cbb6eddd3dd9d552e0d1e44e16: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen50172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50173" type="x-p"/> But that he also descended - The meaning of the apostle appears to be this: The person who ascended is the Messiah, and his ascension plainly intimates his descension; that is, his incarnation, humiliation, death, and resurrection.
entries.eac99ed7325b66b833e5f587a4ce23aaeea3d18f: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen50173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50174" type="x-p"/> He that descended - And he who descended so low is the same who has ascended so high. He came to the lower parts of the earth - the very deepest abasement; having emptied himself; taken upon him; the form of a servant, and humbled himself unto death, even the death of the cross; now he is ascended far above all heavens - higher than all height; he has a name above every name. Here his descending into the lower parts of the earth is put in opposition to his ascending far above all heavens. His abasement was unparalleled; so also is his exaltation. <div eID="gen50174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50175" type="x-p"/> That he might fill all things - That he might be the fountain whence all blessings might flow; dispensing all good things to all his creatures, according to their several capacities and necessities; and, particularly, fill both converted Jews and Gentiles with all the gifts and graces of his Holy Spirit. Hence it follows:
entries.a51512b08e6043d3a6a140cd1beccf4845c607d7: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen50175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50176" type="x-p"/> He gave some, apostles - He established several offices in his Church; furnished these with the proper officers; and, to qualify them for their work, gave them the proper gifts. For a full illustration of this verse, the reader is requested to refer to the notes on <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.6-1Cor.12.10">1Cor 12:6-10</reference> (note), <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.28-1Cor.12.30">1Cor 12:28-30</reference> (note); and to the concluding observations at the end of that chapter.
entries.f69344b89c0daabe31349459fb7500a8f7ac0942: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen50176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50177" type="x-p"/> For the perfecting of the saints - For the complete instruction, purification, and union of all who have believed in Christ Jesus, both Jews and Gentiles. For the meaning of καταρτισμος, perfecting, see the note on <reference osisRef="2Cor.13.9">2Cor 13:9</reference>. <div eID="gen50177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50178" type="x-p"/> For the work of the ministry - All these various officers, and the gifts and graces conferred upon them, were judged necessary, by the great Head of the Church, for its full instruction in the important doctrines of Christianity. The same officers and gifts are still necessary, and God gives them; but they do not know their places. In most Christian Churches there appears to be but one office, that of preacher; and one gift, that by which he professes to preach. The apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors, and teachers, are all compounded in the class preachers; and many, to whom God has given nothing but the gift of exhortation, take texts to explain them; and thus lose their time, and mar their ministry. <div eID="gen50178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50179" type="x-p"/> Edifying of the body - The body of Christ is his Church, see <reference osisRef="Eph.2.20">Eph 2:20</reference>, etc.; and its edification consists in its thorough instruction in Divine things, and its being filled with faith and holiness.
entries.37b99d289a9edff5532cab72bc081a9f9a1742fc: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen50179" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50180" type="x-p"/> In the unity of the faith - Jews and Gentiles being all converted according to the doctrines laid down in the faith - the Christian system. <div eID="gen50180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50181" type="x-p"/> The knowledge of the Son of God - A trite understanding of the mystery of the incarnation; why God was manifest in the flesh, and why this was necessary in order to human salvation. <div eID="gen50181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50182" type="x-p"/> Unto a perfect man - Εις ανδρα τελειον· One thoroughly instructed; the whole body of the Church being fully taught, justified, sanctified, and sealed. <div eID="gen50182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50183" type="x-p"/> Measure of the stature - The full measure of knowledge, love, and holiness, which the Gospel of Christ requires. Many preachers, and multitudes of professing people, are studious to find out how many imperfections and infidelities, and how much inward sinfulness, is consistent with a safe state in religion but how few, very few, are bringing out the fair Gospel standard to try the height of the members of the Church; whether they be fit for the heavenly army; whether their stature be such as qualifies them for the ranks of the Church militant! The measure of the stature of the fullness is seldom seen; the measure of the stature of littleness, dwarfishness, and emptiness, is often exhibited.
entries.b0bff3760baa96b6030ef7e6419124b653a3d317: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen50183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50184" type="x-p"/> Be no more children - Children, here, are opposed to the perfect man in the preceding verse; and the state of both is well explained by the apostle's allusions. The man is grown up strong and healthy, and has attained such a measure or height as qualifies him for the most respectable place in the ranks of his country. <div eID="gen50184" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50185" type="x-p"/> The child is ignorant, weak, and unsteady, tossed about in the nurse's arms, or whirled round in the giddy sports or mazes of youth; this seems to be the apostle's allusion. Being tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine, refers to some kind of ancient play, but what I cannot absolutely determine; probably to something similar to a top, or to our paper kite. <div eID="gen50185" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50186" type="x-p"/> By the sleight of men - The words εν τη κυβειᾳ refer to the arts used by gamesters, who employ false dice that will always throw up one kind of number, which is that by which those who play with them cannot win. <div eID="gen50186" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50187" type="x-p"/> Cunning craftiness - It is difficult to give a literal translation of the original words: εν πανουργιᾳ προς την μεθοδειαν της πλανης· "By cunning, for the purpose of using the various means of deception." Πανουργια signifies craft and subtlety in general, cheating and imposition: μεθοδεια, from which we have our term method, signifies a wile, a particular sleight, mode of tricking and deceiving; it is applied to the arts which the devil uses to deceive and destroy souls; see <reference osisRef="Eph.6.11">Eph 6:11</reference>, called there the Wiles of the devil. From this it seems that various arts were used, both by the Greek sophists and the Judaizing teachers, to render the Gospel of none effect, or to adulterate and corrupt it.
entries.d596071899a7e549b25ca2eeb9899cacba38073b: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen50187" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50188" type="x-p"/> But, speaking the truth in love - The truth recommended by the apostle is the whole system of Gospel doctrine; this they are to teach and preach, and this is opposed to the deceit mentioned above. This truth, as it is the doctrine of God's eternal love to mankind, must be preached in love. Scolding and abuse from the pulpit or press, in matters of religion, are truly monstrous. He who has the truth of God has no need of any means to defend or propagate it, but those which love to God and man provides. <div eID="gen50188" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50189" type="x-p"/> Grow up into him - This is a continuance of the metaphor taken from the members of a human body receiving nourishment equally and growing up, each in its due proportion to other parts, and to the body in general. The truth of God should be so preached to all the members of the Church of God, that they may all receive an increase of grace and life; so that each, in whatever state he may be, may get forward in the way of truth and holiness. In the Church of Christ there are persons in various states: the careless, the penitent, the lukewarm, the tempted, the diffident, the little child, the young man, and the father. He who has got a talent for the edification of only one of those classes should not stay long in a place, else the whole body cannot grow up in all things under his ministry.
entries.17a3cddda2f8bb1be1874666cdb0666e22dc2971: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen50189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50190" type="x-p"/> From whom the whole body - Dr. Macknight has a just view of this passage, and I cannot express my own in more suitable terms: "The apostle's meaning is, that, as the human body is formed by the union of all the members to each other, under the head, and by the fitness of each member for its own office and place in the body, so the Church is formed by the union of its members under Christ, the head. Farther, as the human body increases till it arrives at maturity by the energy of every part in performing its proper function, and by the sympathy of every part with the whole, so the body or Church of Christ grows to maturity by the proper exercise of the gifts and graces of individuals for the benefit of the whole." <div eID="gen50190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50191" type="x-p"/> This verse is another proof of the wisdom and learning of the apostle. Not only the general ideas here are anatomical, but the whole phraseology is the same. The articulation of the bones, the composition and action of the muscles, the circulation of the fluids, carrying nourishment to every part, and depositing some in every place, the energy of the system in keeping up all the functions, being particularly introduced, and the whole terminating in the general process of nutrition, increasing the body, and supplying all the waste that had taken place in consequence of labor, etc. Let any medical man, who understands the apostle's language, take up this verse, and he will be convinced that the apostle had all these things in view. I am surprised that some of those who have looked for the discoveries of the moderns among the ancients, have not brought in the apostle's word επιχορηγια , supply, from επιχορηγεω, to lead up, lead along, minister, supply, etc., as some proof that the circulation of the blood was not unknown to St. Paul!
entries.ae4c454fee35b84b300e9074a5c0a3ea70175a62: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen50191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50192" type="x-p"/> Walk not as other Gentiles walk - Ye are called to holiness by the Gospel, the other Gentiles have no such calling; walk not as they walk. In this and the two following verses the apostle gives a most awful account of the conduct of the heathens who were without the knowledge of the true God. I shall note the particulars. <div eID="gen50192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50193" type="x-p"/> 1. They walked in the vanity of their mind, εν ματαιοτητι του νοος αὑτων· In the foolishness of their mind; want of genuine wisdom is that to which the apostle refers, and it was through this that the Gentiles became addicted to every species of idolatry; and they fondly imagined that they could obtain help from gods which were the work of their own hands! Here their foolishness was manifested.
entries.29464376d99effb053f2fc182887985a542bf42c: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen50193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50194" type="x-p"/> 2. Having the understanding darkened - This is the second instance alleged by the apostle of the degradation of the Gentiles. Having no means of knowledge, the heart, naturally dark, became more and more so by means of habitual transgression; every thing in the Gentile system having an immediate tendency to blind the eyes and darken the whole soul. <div eID="gen50194" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50195" type="x-p"/> 3. Being alienated from the life of God - The original design of God was to live in man; and the life of God in the soul of man was that by which God intended to make man happy, and without which true happiness was never found by any human spirit: from this through the ignorance that was in them, δια την αγνοιαν την ουσαν, through the substantial or continually existing ignorance, which there was nothing to instruct, nothing to enlighten; for the most accurate writings of their best philosophers left them entirely ignorant of the real nature of God. And if they had no correct knowledge of the true God they could have no religion; and if no religion, no morality. Their moral state became so wretched that they are represented as abhorring every thing spiritual and pure, for this is the import of the word απηλλοτριωμενοι (which we translate alienated) in some of the best Greek writers. They abhorred every thing that had a tendency to lay any restraint on their vicious passions and inclinations. <div eID="gen50195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50196" type="x-p"/> 4. Blindness of their heart - Δια την πωρωσιν· Because of the callousness of their hearts. Callous signifies a thickening of the outward skin of any particular part, especially on the hands and feet, by repeated exercise or use, through which such parts are rendered insensible. This may be metaphorically applied to the conscience of a sinner, which is rendered stupid and insensible by repeated acts of iniquity.
entries.a1ae973d58c0a9970ce0e3adb8601949b39520ac: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen50196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50197" type="x-p"/> 5. Who being past feeling - Οιτινες απηλγηκοτες. The verb απαλγειν signifies, <div eID="gen50197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50198" type="x-p"/> 1. To throw off all sense of shame, and to be utterly devoid of pain, for committing unrighteous acts. <div eID="gen50198" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50199" type="x-p"/> 2. To be desperate, having neither hope nor desire of reformation; in a word, to be without remorse, and to be utterly regardless of conduct, character, or final blessedness. <div eID="gen50199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50200" type="x-p"/> Instead of απηλγηκοτες, several excellent MSS. and versions have απηλπικοτες, being without hope; that is, persons who, from their manner of life in this world, could not possibly hope for blessedness in the world to come, and who might feel it their interest to deny the resurrection of the body, and even the immortality of the soul. <div eID="gen50200" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50201" type="x-p"/> 6. Have given themselves over unto lasciviousness - Lasciviousness, ασελγεια, is here personified; and the Gentiles in question are represented as having delivered themselves over to her jurisdiction. This is a trite picture of the Gentile world: uncleanness, lechery, and debauchery of every kind, flourished among them without limit or restraint. Almost all their gods and goddesses were of this character. <div eID="gen50201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50202" type="x-p"/> 7. To work all uncleanness with greediness - This is a complete finish of the most abandoned character; to do an unclean act is bad, to labor in it is worse, to labor in all uncleanness is worse still; but to do all this in every case to the utmost extent, εν πλεονεξια, with a desire exceeding time, place, opportunity, and strength, is worst of all, and leaves nothing more profligate or more abandoned to be described or imagined; just as Ovid paints the drunken Silenus, whose wantonness survives his strength and keeps alive his desires, though old age has destroyed the power of gratification: - <div eID="gen50202" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50203" type="x-p"/> Te quoque, inextinctae Silene libidinis, urunt: <div eID="gen50203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50204" type="x-p"/> Nequitia est, quae te non sinit esse senem. <div eID="gen50204" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50205" type="x-p"/> Fast., lib. i. v. 413. <div eID="gen50205" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50206" type="x-p"/> Thee also, O Silenus, of inextinguishable lust, they inflame; Thou art old in every thing except in lust. <div eID="gen50206" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50207" type="x-p"/> Such was the state of the Gentiles before they were blessed with the light of the Gospel; and such is the state of those nations who have not yet received the Gospel; and such is the state of multitudes of those in Christian countries who refuse to receive the Gospel, endeavor to decry it, and to take refuge in the falsities of infidelity against the testimony of eternal truth.
entries.9cad01c7fc13897418bedff66d96d2ead2d0acd5: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen50207" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50208" type="x-p"/> But ye have not so learned Christ - Ye have received the doctrines of Christianity, and therefore are taught differently; ye have received the Spirit of Christ, and therefore are saved from such dispositions. Some would point and translate the original thus: Ὑμεις δε ουχ οὑτως· εμαθετε τον Χριστον· But ye are not thus; ye have learned Christ.
entries.f9ab9eb2d89cf1917aef614792a4a724ae4c5aec: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen50208" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50209" type="x-p"/> If so be that ye have heard him - Ειγε, Seeing that, since indeed, ye have heard us proclaim his eternal truth; we have delivered it to you as we received it from Jesus.
entries.a4581b510c51eafe1051b1937ebae7030e6ba8dd: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen50209" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50210" type="x-p"/> That ye put off - And this has been one especial part of our teaching, that ye should abandon all these, and live a life totally opposite to what it was before. <div eID="gen50210" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50211" type="x-p"/> The old man - See the note on <reference osisRef="Rom.6.6">Rom 6:6</reference>, and especially see the notes on <reference osisRef="Rom.13.13">Rom 13:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.13.14">Rom 13:14</reference> (note). <div eID="gen50211" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50212" type="x-p"/> Which is corrupt - The whole of your former life was corrupt and abominable; ye lived in the pursuit of pleasure and happiness; ye sought this in the gratification of the lusts of the flesh; and were ever deceived by these lusts, and disappointed in your expectations.
entries.975227927b175724169e6c2bad816ae5cb38182d: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen50212" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50213" type="x-p"/> And be renewed in the spirit of your mind - Their old mode of living was to be abandoned; a new one to be assumed. The mind is to be renovated; and not only its general complexion, but the very spirit of it; all its faculties and powers must be thoroughly, completely, and universally renewed. Plautus uses a similar expression describing deep distress, and answerable to our phrase innermost soul: - <div eID="gen50213" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50214" type="x-p"/> Paupertas, pavor territat mentem animi. <div eID="gen50214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50215" type="x-p"/> Poverty and dread alarm my innermost soul. <div eID="gen50215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50216" type="x-p"/> Epid., l. 519.
entries.36568679b010ae8a66ed9657c73675475b216517: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen50216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50217" type="x-p"/> Put on the new man - Get a new nature; for in Christ Jesus - under the Christian dispensation, neither circumcision avails any thing, nor uncircumcision, hut a new creation. Therefore ye must be renewed in the spirit of your mind. <div eID="gen50217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50218" type="x-p"/> Which after God is created in righteousness - Here is certainly an allusion to the creation of man. Moses tells us, <reference osisRef="Gen.1.27">Gen 1:27</reference>, that God created man in his own image; that is, God was the model according to which he was formed in the spirit of his mind. St. Paul says here that they should put on the new man, which after God is created in righteousness and true holiness, or, ὁσιοτητι της αληθειας, in the holiness of truth. Both certainly refer to the same thing, and the one illustrates the other. From the apostle we learn what Moses meant by the image of God; it was righteousness and the truth of holiness. See the note on <reference osisRef="Gen.1.26">Gen 1:26</reference>. It is not this or the other degree of moral good which the soul is to receive by Jesus Christ, it is the whole image of God; it is to be formed κατα Θεον, according to God; the likeness of the Divine Being is to be traced upon his soul, and he is to bear that as fully as his first father Adam bore it in the beginning.
entries.5fafe7080b54b858159857abec10a43a88cf55c7: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen50218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50219" type="x-p"/> Wherefore putting away lying - All falsity, all prevarication, because this is opposite to the truth as it is in Jesus, <reference osisRef="Eph.4.21">Eph 4:21</reference>, and to the holiness of truth, <reference osisRef="Eph.4.24">Eph 4:24</reference>. <div eID="gen50219" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50220" type="x-p"/> Speak every man truth with his neighbor - Truth was but of small account among many of even the best heathens, for they taught that on many occasions a lie was to be preferred to the truth itself. Dr. Whitby collects some of their maxims on this head. Κρειττον δε ελεσθαι ψευδος, η αληθες κακον· "A lie is better than a hurtful truth." - Menander. Το γαρ αγαθον κρειττον εστι της αληθειας· "Good is better than truth." - Proclus. Ενθα γαρ τι δει και ψευδος λεγεσθαι, λεγεσθω. "When telling a lie will be profitable, let it be told." - Darius in Herodotus, lib. iii. p. 101. "He may lie who knows how to do it εν δεοντι καιρῳ, in a suitable time." - Plato apud Stob., ser. 12. "There is nothing decorous in truth but when it is profitable; yea, sometimes και ψευδος ωνησεν ανθρωπους, και τ' αληθες εβλαψεν, truth is hurtful, and lying is profitable to men." - Maximus Tyrius, Diss. 3, p. 29. <div eID="gen50220" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50221" type="x-p"/> Having been brought up in such a loose system of morality, these converted Gentiles had need of these apostolic directions; Put away lying; speak the truth: Let lying never come near you; let truth be ever present with you. <div eID="gen50221" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50222" type="x-p"/> We are members one of another - Consider yourselves as one body, of which Jesus Christ is the head; and as a man's right hand would not deceive or wrong his left hand, so deal honestly with each other; for ye are members one of another.
entries.5f2f33cb6c41bd2800fd298f83c9fa06608aa253: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen50222" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50223" type="x-p"/> Be ye angry, and sin not - Οργιζεσθε, here, is the same as ει μεν οργιζεσθε, If Ye be angry, do not sin. We can never suppose that the apostle delivers this as a precept, if we take the words as they stand in our version. Perhaps the sense is, Take heed that ye be not angry, lest ye sin; for it would be very difficult, even for an apostle himself, to be angry and not sin. If we consider anger as implying displeasure simply, then there are a multitude of cases in which a man may be innocently, yea, laudably angry; for he should be displeased with every thing which is not for the glory of God, and the good of mankind. But, in any other sense, I do not see how the words can be safely taken. <div eID="gen50223" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50224" type="x-p"/> Let not the sun go down upon your wrath - That is: If you do get angry with any one, see that the fire be cast with the utmost speed out of your bosom. Do not go to sleep with any unkind or unbrotherly feeling; anger, continued in, may produce malice and revenge. No temper of this kind can consist with peace of conscience, and the approbation of God's Spirit in the soul.
entries.8f392e195781482db592f152c4dd6335211c4d77: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen50224" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50225" type="x-p"/> Neither give place to the devil - Your adversary will strive to influence your mind, and irritate your spirit; watch and pray that he may not get any place in you, or ascendancy over you. <div eID="gen50225" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50226" type="x-p"/> As the word διαβολος is sometimes used to signify a calumniator, tale-bearer, whisperer, or backbiter; (see in the original, <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.11">1Tim 3:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.3">2Tim 3:3</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Tit.2.3">Tit 2:3</reference>); here it may have the same signification. Do not open your ear to the tale-bearer, to the slanderer, who comes to you with accusations against your brethren, or with surmisings and evil speakings. These are human devils; they may be the means of making you angry, even without any solid pretense; therefore give them no place, that you may not be angry at any time; but if, unhappily, you should be overtaken in this fault, let not the sun go down upon your wrath; go to your brother, against whom you have found your spirit irritated; tell him what you have heard, and what you fear; let your ears be open to receive his own account; carefully listen to his own explanation; and, if possible, let the matter be finally settled, that Satan may not gain advantage over either.
entries.820745b1e41683672c9bb07704d4a48e36a6d1a8: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen50226" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50227" type="x-p"/> Let him that stole steal no more - It is supposed that, among the rabbins, stealing was not entirely discountenanced, provided a portion was given to the poor. The apostle here teaches them a different doctrine: as they should speak truth every man with his neighbor, so they should in every respect act honestly, for nothing contrary to truth and righteousness could be tolerated under the Christian system. Let no man, under pretense of helping the poor, defraud another; but let him labor, working with his hands to provide that which is good, that he may have to give to him who is in necessity. Stealing, overreaching, defrauding, purloining, etc., are consistent with no kind of religion that acknowledges the true God. If Christianity does not make men honest, it does nothing for them. Those who are not saved from dishonesty fear not God, though they may dread man.
entries.f9ad45385918551b5ec0b66c21e204ae9ba492e3: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen50227" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50228" type="x-p"/> Let no corrupt communication - Πας λογος σαπρος. Kypke observes that λογος σαπρος signifies a useless, putrid, unsavory, and obscene word or conversation. <div eID="gen50228" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50229" type="x-p"/> 1. Useless, particularly that which has been rendered so by old age and corruption. <div eID="gen50229" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50230" type="x-p"/> 2. Putrid, impure; so Aristophanes in Lysistrat., p. 859, calls a bad woman σαπρα: εμοι συ λουτρον, ω σαπρα· Tune, Spurca! balneum mihi parabis? <div eID="gen50230" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50231" type="x-p"/> 3. Calumnious, or reproachful; whatever has a tendency to injure the name, fame, or interest of another. <div eID="gen50231" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50232" type="x-p"/> In short, it appears to mean any word or thing obscene, any thing that injures virtue, countenances vice, or scoffs at religion. In the parallel place, <reference osisRef="Col.4.6">Col 4:6</reference>, the apostle exhorts that our speech may be seasoned with salt, to preserve it from putrefaction. See Kypke and Macknight. <div eID="gen50232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50233" type="x-p"/> But that which is good to the use of edifying - To be good for a thing is a Graecism, as well as an Anglicism, for, to be fit, proper, suitable, etc.; so Achilles Tatius, lib. iv. p. 231: Αγαθον εις φιλιαν οιδα σε· I know thee to be good (formed) for friendship. And Appian, de Bell. Hisp., p. 439, terms both the Scipios, Ανδρας ες παντα αγαθους γενομενους, men who were good (suitable) for all things. And also Lucian, in Toxari, p. 53: Ου μονον αρα τοξευειν αγαθοι ησαν Σκυθαι· The Scythians were not good (expert) in archery only. See Kypke, from whom I quote. <div eID="gen50233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50234" type="x-p"/> That it may minister grace - Ἱνα δῳ χαριν. This may be understood thus: <div eID="gen50234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50235" type="x-p"/> 1. Let your conversation be pure, wise, and holy, that it may he the means of conveying grace, or Divine influences, to them that hear. <div eID="gen50235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50236" type="x-p"/> 2. Let it be such as to be grateful or acceptable to the hearers. This is the meaning of Ἱνα δῳ χαριν in some of the most correct Greek writers. Never wound modesty, truth, or religion with your discourse; endeavor to edify those with whom you converse; and if possible, speak so as to please them.
entries.1a388ad721f942135090e200caf162675dcb1087: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen50236" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50237" type="x-p"/> Grieve not the Holy Spirit of God - By giving way to any wrong temper, unholy word, or unrighteous action. Even those who have already a measure of the light and life of God, both of which are not only brought in by the Holy Spirit, but maintained by his constant indwelling, may give way to sin, and so grieve this Holy Spirit that it shall withdraw both its light and presence; and, in proportion as it withdraws, then hardness and darkness take place; and, what is still worse, a state of insensibility is the consequence; for the darkness prevents the fallen state from being seen, and the hardness prevents it from being felt. <div eID="gen50237" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50238" type="x-p"/> Whereby ye are sealed - The Holy Spirit in the soul of a believer is God's seal, set on his heart to testify that he is God's property, and that he should be wholly employed in God's service. It is very likely that the apostle had in view the words of the prophet, <reference osisRef="Isa.63.10">Isa 63:10</reference> : But they rebelled, and Vexed his Holy Spirit; therefore he was turned to be their enemy, and fought against them. The psalmist refers to the same fact in nearly the same words, <reference osisRef="Psa.78.40">Psa 78:40</reference> : How oft did they Provoke him in the wilderness, and Grieve him in the desert! Let every man, therefore, take heed that he grieve not the Spirit of God, lest God turn to be his enemy, and fight against him.
entries.50a4a27f4fc52ad707a38b9816a6b7015d3b57ae: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen50238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50239" type="x-p"/> Let all bitterness - Πασα πικρια. It is astonishing that any who profess the Christian name should indulge bitterness of spirit. Those who are censorious, who are unmerciful to the failings of others, who have fixed a certain standard by which they measure all persons in all circumstances, and unchristian every one that does not come up to this standard, these have the bitterness against which the apostle speaks. In the last century there was a compound medicine, made up from a variety of drastic acrid drugs and ardent spirits, which was called Hiera Picra, ἱερα πικρα, the holy bitter; this medicine was administered in a multitude of cases, where it did immense evil, and perhaps in scarcely any case did it do good. It has ever appeared to me to furnish a proper epithet for the disposition mentioned above, the holy bitter; for the religiously censorious act under the pretense of superior sanctity. I have known such persons do much evil in a Christian society, but never knew an instance of their doing any good. <div eID="gen50239" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50240" type="x-p"/> And wrath - Θυμος is more properly anger, which may be considered the commencement of the passion. <div eID="gen50240" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50241" type="x-p"/> Anger - Οργν is more properly wrath - the passion carried to its highest pitch, accompanied with injurious words and outrageous acts, some of which are immediately specified. <div eID="gen50241" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50242" type="x-p"/> And clamor - Κραυγη Loud and obstreperous speaking, brawling, railing, boisterous talk, often the offspring of wrath; all of which are highly unbecoming the meek, loving, quiet, sedate mind of Christ and his followers. <div eID="gen50242" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50243" type="x-p"/> And evil speaking - Βλασφημια· Blasphemy; that is, injurious speaking - words which tend to hurt those of whom or against whom they are spoken. <div eID="gen50243" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50244" type="x-p"/> With all malice - Κακια· All malignity; as anger produces wrath, and wrath clamor, so all together produce malice; that is, settled, sullen, fell wrath, which is always looking out for opportunities to revenge itself by the destruction of the object of its indignation. No state of society can be even tolerable where these prevail; and, if eternity were out of the question, it is of the utmost consequence to have these banished from time.
entries.f693bee4f3cc67beb0286eb30146216a670d5834: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen50244" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50245" type="x-p"/> Be ye kind one to another - Γινεσθε - χρηστοι· Be kind and obliging to each other; study good breeding and gentleness of manners. A Christian cannot be a savage, and he need not be a boor. Never put any person to needless pain. <div eID="gen50245" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50246" type="x-p"/> Tender-hearted - Ευσπλαγχνοι· Compassionate; having the bowels easily moved (as the word implies) to commiserate the state of the wretched and distressed. <div eID="gen50246" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50247" type="x-p"/> Forgiving one another - Should you receive any injury from a brother, or from any man, be as ready to forgive him, on his repentance and acknowledgment, as God was, for Christ's sake, to forgive you when you repented of your sins, and took refuge in his mercy. <div eID="gen50247" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50248" type="x-p"/> 1. The exhortations given in this chapter, if properly attended to, have the most direct tendency to secure the peace of the individual, the comfort of every family, and the welfare and unity of every Christian society. That God never prohibits any thing that is useful to us, is an unshaken truth. And that he never commands what has not the most pointed relation to our present and eternal welfare, is not less so. How is it, then, that we do not glory in his commandments and rejoice in his prohibitions?
