Again, we see that no man is excepted; all are enjoined to be subject, and to take their own places in the body.<div eID="gen125076" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen125077" type="x-p"/>What aspect then does Popery present, but that of a crooked, deformed person? Is not the whole symmetry of the church destroyed, when one man, acting in opposition to the head, refuses to be reckoned one of the members? The Papists deny this, and allege that the Pope is nothing more than a ministerial head. But such cavils do them no service. The tyranny of their idol must be acknowledged to be altogether inconsistent with that order which Paul here recommends. In a word, a healthful condition of the church requires that Christ alone “must increase,” and all others “must decrease.” (<reference osisRef="Bible:John.3.30">John 3:30</reference>.) Whatever increase we obtain must be regulated in such a manner, that we shall remain in our own place, and contribute to exalt the head.<div eID="gen125077" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen125078" type="x-p"/>When he bids us give heed to the truth <hi type="italic">in love,</hi> he uses the preposition <hi type="italic">in</hi>, (ἐν,) like the corresponding Hebrew preposition <foreign xml:lang="he">ב</foreign>, (<hi type="italic">beth</hi>,) as signifying <hi type="italic">with</hi>, — <hi type="italic">speaking the truth With love</hi> <note n="146"> <div sID="gen125079" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="el"> ᾿Αλγθεύοντες ἐν ἀγάπη</foreign>, means much more than ‘<hi type="italic">speaking</hi> the truth in love;’ it signifies thinking, feeling, acting under the influence of ‘the truth, which worketh by love.’” — Brown.<div eID="gen125079" type="x-p"/> </note> If each individual, instead of attending exclusively to his own concerns, shall desire mutual intercourse, there will be agreeable and general progress. Such, the Apostle assures us, must be the nature of this harmony, that men shall not be suffered to forget the claims of truth, or, disregarding them, to frame an agreement according to their own views. This proves the wickedness of the Papists, who lay aside the word of God, and labor to force our compliance with their decisions.<div eID="gen125078" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Eph.4.15" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen125073" osisID="Eph.4.15" type="section"/>
entries.d95b02e1bfbd0879d066326ef37c787d4915a1a4:
16. From whom the whole body. All our increase should tend to exalt more highly the glory of Christ. This is now proved by the best possible reason. It is he who supplies all our wants, and without whose protection we cannot be safe. As the root conveys sap to the whole tree, so all the vigor which we possess must flow to us from Christ. There are three things here which deserve our attention. The first is what has now been stated. All the life or health which is diffused through the members flows from the head; so that the members occupy a subordinate rank. The second is, that, by the distribution made, the limited share of each renders the communication between all the members absolutely necessary. The third is, that, without mutual love, the health of the body cannot be maintained. Through the members, as canals, is conveyed from the head all that is necessary for the nourishment of the body. While this connection is upheld, the body is alive and healthy. Each member, too, has its own proper share, — according to the effectual working in the measure of every part.
Lastly, he shows that by love the church is edified, — to the edifying of itself in love. This means that no increase is advantageous, which does not bear a just proportion to the whole body. That man is mistaken who desires his own separate growth. If a leg or arm should grow to a prodigious size, or the mouth be more fully distended, would the undue enlargement of those parts be otherwise than injurious to the whole frame? In like manner, if we wish to be considered members of Christ, let no man be anything for himself, but let us all be whatever we are for the benefit of each other. This is accomplished by love; and where it does not reign, there is no “edification,” but an absolute scattering of the church.
Ephesians 4:17-19
17. This I say therefore, and testify in the Lord, that ye henceforth walk not as other Gentiles walk, in the vanity of their mind;
17. Hoc ergo dico et testificor in Domino, ne ambuletis amplius, quemadmodum et gentes reliquae ambulant,
18. Having the understanding darkened, being alienated from the life of God through the ignorance that is in them, because of the blindness of their heart:
18. In vanitate mentis suae, excaecatae in intelligentia, alienatae a vita Dei propter ignorantiam, quae in illis est, propter caecitatem cordis earum;
19. Who, being past feeling, have given themselves over unto lasciviousness, to work all uncleanness with greediness.
19. Quae postquam dolore tangi desierunt, seipsas tradiderunt lasciviae, ad perpetrandam omnem immunditiam cum aviditate.
entries.bdf8ffbc10163d3b96f92f4b5e3491dc5329565d: <div annotateRef="Bible:Eph.4.17" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Eph.4.17" sID="gen125092" type="section"/> <div sID="gen125093" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">17.</hi><hi type="italic"> This I say therefore.</hi> That government which Christ has appointed for the edification of his church has now been considered. He next inquires what fruits the doctrine of the gospel ought to yield in the lives of Christians; or, if you prefer it, he begins to explain minutely the nature of that edification by which doctrine ought to be followed.<div eID="gen125093" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen125094" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">That ye henceforth walk not in vanity.</hi> He first exhorts them to renounce the <hi type="italic">vanity</hi> of unbelievers, arguing from its inconsistency with their present views. That those who have been taught in the school of Christ, and enlightened by the doctrine of salvation, should follow vanity, and in no respect differ from those unbelieving and blind nations on whom no light of truth has ever shone, would be singularly foolish. On this ground he very properly calls upon them to demonstrate, by their life, that they had gained some advantage by becoming the disciples of Christ. To impart to his exhortation the greater earnestness, he beseeches them by the name of God, — <hi type="italic">this I say and testify in the Lord,</hi> <note n="147"> <div sID="gen125095" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="el">Μαρτύρομαι ἐν κυρίῳ</foreign> — In this sense <foreign xml:lang="el">μαρτύρομαι</foreign> is obviously used by Polybius: <foreign xml:lang="el">συνδαραμόντων δὲ τῶν ἐγχωρίων καὶ μαρτυρομένων τοὺς ἄνδρας ἐπανάγειν ἐπὶ τὴν ἀρχήν</foreign>, when the inhabitants had run together and besought to bring the men to the magistrates. It is more customary to use <foreign xml:lang="el">διαμαρτύρομαι</foreign> in this sense. <foreign xml:lang="el">Πολλὰ γὰρ τῶν κυβερνητῶν διαμαρτυρομένων μὴ πλεῖν παρὰ τὴν ἔξω πλευρὰν τὢς Σικελίας</foreign>, because the pilots earnestly implored them not to sail along the opposite coast of Sicily.” — Raphelius.<div eID="gen125095" type="x-p"/> </note> — reminding them, that, if they despised this instruction, they must one day give an account.<div eID="gen125094" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen125096" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">As other Gentiles walk.</hi> He means those who had not yet been converted to Christ. But, at the same time, he reminds the Ephesians how necessary it was that they should repent, since by nature they resembled lost and condemned men. The miserable and shocking condition of other nations is held out as the motive to a change of disposition. He asserts that believers differ from unbelievers; and points out, as we shall see, the causes of this difference. With regard to the former, he accuses their mind of <hi type="italic">vanity:</hi> and let us remember, that he speaks generally of all who have not been renewed by the Spirit of Christ.<div eID="gen125096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen125097" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">In the vanity of their mind.</hi> Now, <hi type="italic">the mind</hi> holds the highest rank in the human constitution, is the seat of reason, presides over the will, and restrains sinful desires; so that our theologians of the <hi type="italic">Sorbonne</hi> are in the habit of calling her the Queen. But, Paul makes the <hi type="italic">mind</hi> to consist of nothing else than vanity; and, as if he had not expressed his meaning strongly enough, he gives no better title to her daughter, <hi type="italic">the understanding.</hi> Such is my interpretation of the word διανοία; for, though it signifies the thought, yet, as it is in the singular number, it refers to the thinking faculty. Plato, about the close of his Sixth Book on a Republic, assigns to διανοία an intermediate place between νόησις and πίστις but his observations are so entirely confined to geometrical subjects, as not to admit of application to this passage. Having formerly asserted that men see nothing, Paul now adds, that they are blind in reasoning, even on the most important subjects.<div eID="gen125097" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen125098" type="x-p"/>Let men now go and be proud of free-will, whose guidance is here marked by so deep disgrace. But experience, we shall be told, is openly at variance with this opinion; for men are not so blind as to be incapable of seeing anything, nor so vain as to be incapable of forming any judgment. I answer, with respect to the kingdom of God, and all that relates to the spiritual life, the light of human reason differs little from darkness; for, before it has pointed out the road, it is extinguished; and its power of perception is little else than blindness, for ere it has reached the fruit, it is gone. The true principles held by the human mind resemble sparks; <note n="148"> <div sID="gen125099" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Il y a bien en l’esprit de l’homme des principes et maximes veritables, qui sont commes estincelles</foreign>.” “There are, in the mind of man, many true principles and maxims, which resemble sparks.”<div eID="gen125099" type="x-p"/> </note> but these are choked by the depravity of our nature, before they have been applied to their proper use. All men know, for instance, that there is a God, and that it is our duty to worship him; but such is the power of sin and ignorance, that from this confused knowledge we pass all at once to an idol, and worship it in the place of God. And even in the worship of God, it leads to great errors, particularly in the first table of the law.<div eID="gen125098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen125100" type="x-p"/>As to the second objection, our judgment does indeed agree with the law of God in regard to the mere outward actions; but sinful desire, which is the source of everything evil, escapes our notice. Besides, Paul does not speak merely of the natural blindness which we brought with us from the womb, but refers also to a still grosser blindness, by which, as we shall afterwards see, God punishes former transgressions. We conclude with observing, that the reason and understanding which men naturally possess, make them in the sight of God without excuse; but, so long as they allow themselves to live according to their natural disposition, they can only wander, and fall, and stumble in their purposes and actions. Hence it appears in what estimation and value false worship must appear in the sight of God, when it proceeds from the gulf of vanity and the maze of ignorance.<div eID="gen125100" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Eph.4.17" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen125092" osisID="Eph.4.17" type="section"/>
entries.0bb04566da6cbeed236da63734a3c9a3d6c95bb2: <div annotateRef="Bible:Eph.4.18" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Eph.4.18" sID="gen125101" type="section"/> <div sID="gen125102" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">18.</hi> <hi type="italic">Being alienated from the life of God.</hi> <hi type="italic">The life of God</hi> may either mean what is accounted life in the sight of God, as in that passage,<div eID="gen125102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen125103" type="x-p"/>“they loved the praise of men more than <hi type="italic">the praise of God</hi>,”<lb/> (<reference osisRef="Bible:John.12.43">John 12:43</reference>,)<div eID="gen125103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen125104" type="x-p"/>or, that life which God bestows on his elect by the Spirit of regeneration. In both cases the meaning is the same. Our ordinary life, as men, is nothing more than an empty image of life, not only because it quickly passes, but also because, while we live, our souls, not keeping close to God, are dead. There are three kinds of life in this world. The first is animal life, which consists only of motion and the bodily senses, and which we have in common with the brutes; the second is human life, which we have as the children of Adam; and the third is that supernatural life, which believers alone obtain. And all of them are from God, so that each of them may be called <hi type="italic">the life of God.</hi> As to the first, Paul, in his sermon at Athens, says, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Acts.17.28">Acts 17:28</reference>,) “In him we live, and move, and have our being;” and the Psalmist says,<div eID="gen125104" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen125105" type="x-p"/>“Send forth thy Spirit, and they shall be created; and thou wilt renew the face of the earth.” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.104.30">Psalm 104:30</reference>.)<div eID="gen125105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen125106" type="x-p"/>Of the second Job says,<div eID="gen125106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen125107" type="x-p"/>“Thou hast granted me life, and thy visitation hath preserved my spirit.” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Job.10.12">Job 10:12</reference>.)<div eID="gen125107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen125108" type="x-p"/>But the regeneration of believers is here called, by way of eminence, <hi type="italic">the life of God, </hi>because then does God truly live in us, and we enjoy his life, when he governs us by his Spirit. Of this life all men who are not new creatures in Christ are declared by Paul to be destitute. So long, then, as we remain in the flesh, that is, in ourselves, how wretched must be our condition! We may now form a judgment of all the moral virtues, as they are called; for what sort of actions will that life produce which, Paul affirms, is not the life of God? Before anything good can begin to proceed from us, we must first be renewed by the grace of Christ. This will be the commencement of a true, and, as the phrase is, a <hi type="italic">vital</hi> life.<div eID="gen125108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen125109" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">On account of the ignorance that is in them.</hi> We ought to attend to the reason which is here assigned; for, as the knowledge of God is the true life of the soul, so, on the contrary, ignorance is the death of it. And lest we should adopt the opinion of philosophers, that ignorance, which leads us into mistakes, is only an incidental evil, Paul shews that it has its root <hi type="italic">in the blindness of their heart,</hi> by which he intimates that it dwells in their very nature. The first blindness, therefore, which covers the minds of men, is the punishment of original sin; because Adam, after his revolt, was deprived of the true light of God, in the absence of which there is nothing but fearful darkness.<div eID="gen125109" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Eph.4.18" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen125101" osisID="Eph.4.18" type="section"/>
entries.879ea78123232e65939624cc82985c50777b7a8a:
19. Who being past feeling. The account which had been given of natural depravity is followed by a description of the worst of all evils, brought upon men by their own sinful conduct. Having destroyed the sensibilities of the heart, and allayed the stings of remorse, they abandon themselves to all manner of iniquity. We are by nature corrupt and prone to evil; nay, we are wholly inclined to evil. Those who are destitute of the Spirit of Christ give loose reins to self-indulgence, till fresh offenses, producing others in constant succession, bring down upon them the wrath of God. The voice of God, proclaimed by an accusing conscience, still continues to be heard; but, instead of producing its proper effects, appears rather to harden them against all admonition. On account of such obstinacy, they deserve to be altogether forsaken by God.
The usual symptom of their having been thus forsaken is — the insensibility to pain, which is here described — being past feeling. Unmoved by the approaching judgment of God, whom they offend, they go on at their ease, and fearlessly indulge without restraint in the pleasures of sin. No shame is felt, no regard to character is maintained. The gnawing of a guilty conscience, tormented by the dread of the Divine judgment, may be compared to the porch of hell; but such hardened security as this — is a whirlpool which swallows up and destroys. As Solomon says,
“When the wicked is come to the deep, he despiseth it.” (Proverbs 18:3.)
Most properly, therefore, does Paul exhibit that dreadful example of Divine vengeance, in which men forsaken by God — having laid conscience to sleep, and destroyed all fear of the Divine judgment, — in a word, being past feeling, — surrender themselves with brutal violence to all wickedness. This is not universally the case. Many even of the reprobate are restrained by God, whose infinite goodness prevents the absolute confusion in which the world would otherwise be involved. The consequence is, that such open lust, such unrestrained intemperance, does not appear in all. It is enough that the lives of some present such a mirror, fitted to awaken our alarm lest anything similar should happen to ourselves.
Lasciviousness (ἀσελγείᾳ) appears to me to denote that wantonness with which the flesh indulges in intemperance and licentiousness, when not restrained by the Spirit of God. Uncleanness is put for scandalous enormities of every description. It is added, with greediness. The Greek word πλεονεξία, which is so translated, often signifies covetousness, (Luke 12:15; 2 Peter 2:14,) and is so explained by some in this passage; but I cannot adopt that view. Depraved and wicked desires being insatiable, Paul represents them as attended and followed by greediness, which is the contrary of moderation.
Ephesians 4:20-24
20. But ye have not so learned Christ;
20. Vos autem non ita didicistis Christum;
21. If so be that ye have heard him, and have been taught by him, as the truth is in Jesus:
21. Si quidem ipsum audistis, et in ipso estis edocti, quemadmodum est veritas in Iesu;
22. That ye put off, concerning the former conversation, the old man, which is corrupt according to the deceitful lusts;
22. Ut deponatis, secundum pristinam conversationem, Veterem hominem, qui corrumpitur secundum concupiscentias erroris;
23. And be renewed in the spirit of your mind;
23. Renovemini autem spiritu mentis vestrae,
24. And that ye put on the new man, which after God is created in righteousness and true holiness.
24. Et induatis Novum hominem, qui secundum Deum creatus est, in justitia et sanctitate veritatis.
entries.3cf72d80e8c0bfaea4d413ceae2fdc3a36aa467f: <div annotateRef="Bible:Eph.4.20" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Eph.4.20" sID="gen125129" type="section"/> <div sID="gen125130" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">20.</hi> <hi type="italic">But ye have not.</hi> He now draws a contrast of a Christian life, so as to make it evident how utterly inconsistent it is with the character of a godly man to defile himself regardlessly with the abominations of the Gentiles. Because the Gentiles walk in darkness, therefore they do not distinguish between right and wrong; but those on whom the truth of God shines ought to live in a different manner. That those to whom the vanity of the senses is a rule of life, should yield themselves up to base lusts, is not surprising; but the doctrine of Christ teaches us to renounce our natural dispositions. He whose life differs not from that of unbelievers, has learned nothing of Christ; for the knowledge of Christ cannot be separated from the mortification of the flesh.<div eID="gen125130" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Eph.4.20" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen125129" osisID="Eph.4.20" type="section"/>
entries.e51a52bd4b6057ba1bd4174882d28afde9e1c717: <div annotateRef="Bible:Eph.4.21" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Eph.4.21" sID="gen125131" type="section"/> <div sID="gen125132" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">21.</hi> <hi type="italic">If ye have heard him.</hi> To excite their attention and earnestness the more, he not only tells them that they had <hi type="italic">heard Christ,</hi> but employs a still stronger expression, <hi type="italic">ye have been taught in him,</hi> as if he had said, that this doctrine had not been slightly pointed out, but faithfully delivered and explained.<div eID="gen125132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen125133" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">As the truth is in Jesus.</hi> This contains a reproof of that superficial knowledge of the gospel, by which many are elated, who are wholly unacquainted with newness of life. They think that they are exceedingly wise, but the apostle pronounces it to be a false and mistaken opinion. There is a twofold knowledge of Christ, — one, which is true and genuine, — and another, which is counterfeit and spurious. Not that, strictly speaking, there are two kinds; but most men falsely imagine that they know Christ, while they know nothing but what is carnal. In another Epistle he says,<div eID="gen125133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen125134" type="x-p"/>“If any man be in Christ, let him be a new creature.”<lb/> (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Cor.5.17">2 Corinthians 5:17</reference>.)<div eID="gen125134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen125135" type="x-p"/>So here he affirms that any knowledge of Christ, which is not accompanied by mortification of the flesh, is not true and sincere.<div eID="gen125135" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Eph.4.21" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen125131" osisID="Eph.4.21" type="section"/>
entries.92d0ba1ee9734832b487a370c98a0809a46429b9:
22. That ye put off. He demands from a Christian man repentance, or a new life, which he makes to consist of self-denial and the regeneration of the Holy Spirit. Beginning with the first, he enjoins us to lay aside, or put off the old man, employing the metaphor of garments, which we have already had occasion to explain. The old man, — as we have repeatedly stated, in expounding the sixth chapter of the Epistle to the Romans, and other passages where it occurs, — means the natural disposition which we bring with us from our mother’s womb. In two persons, Adam and Christ, he describes to us what may be called two natures. As we are first born of Adam, the depravity of nature which we derive from him is called the Old man; and as we are born again in Christ, the amendment of this sinful nature is called the New man. In a word, he who desires to put off the old man must renounce his nature. To suppose that the words Old and New contain an allusion to the Old and New Testaments, is exceedingly unphilosophical.
Concerning the former conversation. To make it more evident that this exhortation to the Ephesians was not unnecessary, he reminds them of their former life. “Before Christ revealed himself to your minds, the old man reigned in you; and therefore, if you desire to lay him aside, you must renounce your former life.” Which is corrupted. He describes the old man from the fruits, that is, from the wicked desires, which allure men to destruction; for the word, corrupt, alludes to old age, which is closely allied to corruption. Let us beware of considering the deceitful lusts, as the Papists do, to mean nothing more than the gross and visible lusts, which are generally acknowledged to be base. The word includes also those dispositions which, instead of being censured, are sometimes applauded, — such as ambition, cunning, and everything that proceeds either from self-love or from want of confidence in God.
entries.f803e3776a19b201e1d824062a506bd131badc50: <div annotateRef="Bible:Eph.4.23" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Eph.4.23" sID="gen125139" type="section"/> <div sID="gen125140" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">23.</hi><hi type="italic"> And be renewed.</hi> The second part of the rule for a devout and holy life is to live, not in our own spirit, but in the Spirit of Christ. But what is meant by — <hi type="italic">the spirit of your mind?</hi> I understand it simply to mean, — <hi type="italic">Be renewed,</hi> not only with respect to the inferior appetites or desires, which are manifestly sinful, but with respect also to that part of the soul which is reckoned most noble and excellent. And here again, he brings forward to view that Queen which philosophers are accustomed almost to adore. There is an implied contrast between <hi type="italic">the spirit of our mind</hi> and the Divine and heavenly Spirit, who produces in us another and a new mind. How much there is in us that is sound or uncorrupted may be easily gathered from this passage, which enjoins us to correct chiefly the reason or <hi type="italic">mind,</hi> in which we are apt to imagine that there is nothing but what is virtuous and deserves commendation.<div eID="gen125140" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Eph.4.23" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen125139" osisID="Eph.4.23" type="section"/>
entries.0fee8c25896097eb9924ab1238101247637f5c28:
24. And that ye put on the new man. All that is meant is, “Be renewed in the spirit, or, be renewed within or completely, — beginning with the mind, which appears to be the part most free from all taint of sin.” What is added about the creation, may refer either to the first creation of man, or to the second creation, which is effected by the grace of Christ. Both expositions will be true. Adam was at first created after the image of God, and reflected, as in a mirror, the Divine righteousness; but that image, having been defaced by sin, must now be restored in Christ. The regeneration of the godly is indeed — as we have formerly explained
See Calvin’s Commentary on Corinthians, vol. 2 p. 187.
— nothing else than the formation anew of the image of God in them. There is, no doubt, a far more rich and powerful manifestation of Divine grace in this second creation than in the first; but our highest perfection is uniformly represented in Scripture as consisting in our conformity and resemblance to God. Adam lost the image which he had originally received, and therefore it becomes necessary that it shall be restored to us by Christ. The design contemplated by regeneration is to recall us from our wanderings to that end for which we were created.
In righteousness. If righteousness be taken as a general term for uprightness, holiness will be something higher, or that purity which lies in being devoted to the service of God. I am rather inclined to consider holiness as referring to the first table, and righteousness to the second table, of the law, as in the song of Zacharias,
“That we may serve him in holiness and righteousness, all the days of our life.” (Luke 1:74,75.)
Plato lays down the distinction correctly, that holiness (ὁσιότης) lies in the worship of God, and that the other part, righteousness, (δικαιοσύνη,) bears a reference to men. The genitive, of truth, (τὢς αληθείας,) is put in the place of an adjective, and refers to both terms; so that, while it literally runs, in righteousness and holiness of truth, the meaning is, in true righteousness and holiness. He warns us that both ought to be sincere; because we have to do with God, whom it is impossible to deceive.
Ephesians 4:25-28
25. Wherefore, putting away lying, speak every man truth with his neighbor: for we are members one of another.
25. Quare, deposito mendacio, loquimini veritatem unusquisque cum proximo suo; quia sumus vicissim inter nos membra.
26. Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath:
26. Irascimini, et ne peccetis. (Psalm 4:5.) Sol non occidat super iracundiam vestram:
27. Neither give place to the devil.
27. Et ne detis locum diabolo.
28. Let him that stole steal no more: but rather let him labor, working with his hands the thing which is good, that he may have to give to him that needeth.
28. Qui furabatur, jam non furetur; magis autem laboret, operando quod bonum est manibus, ut habeat quod eroget opus habenti.
entries.f7fcfbe97f0bc48f76e9f16269de4441652efb92: <div annotateRef="Bible:Eph.4.25" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Eph.4.25" sID="gen125158" type="section"/> <div sID="gen125159" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">25.</hi> <hi type="italic">Wherefore, putting away lying.</hi> From this head of doctrine, that is, from the righteousness of the new man, all godly exhortations flow, like streams from a fountain; for if all the precepts which relate to life were collected, yet, without this principle, they would be of little value. Philosophers take a different method; but, in the doctrine of godliness, there is no other way than this for regulating the life. Now, therefore, he comes to lay down particular exhortations, drawn from the general doctrine. Having concluded from the truth of the gospel, that righteousness and holiness ought to be true, he now argues from the general statement to a particular instance, that <hi type="italic">every man should speak truth with his neighbour. Lying</hi> is here put for every kind of deceit, hypocrisy, or cunning; and <hi type="italic">truth</hi> for honest dealing. He demands that every kind of communication between them shall be sincere; and enforces it by this consideration, <hi type="italic">for we are members one of another</hi>. That <hi type="italic">members</hi> should not agree among themselves, — that they should act in a deceitful manner towards each other, is prodigious wickedness.<div eID="gen125159" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Eph.4.25" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen125158" osisID="Eph.4.25" type="section"/>
entries.0b5021c0e757e3fec2a1c604e9cb2d97932f4935: <div annotateRef="Bible:Eph.4.26" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Eph.4.26" sID="gen125160" type="section"/> <div sID="gen125161" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">26.</hi> <hi type="italic">Be ye angry, and sin not.</hi> Whether or not the apostle had in his eye a part of the fourth Psalm is uncertain. The words used by him (᾿Οργίζεσθε καὶ υὴ ἁμαρτάνετε) occur in the Greek translation, though the word ὀργίζεσθε, which is translated, <hi type="italic">be ye angry,</hi> is considered by some to mean <hi type="italic">tremble. </hi> <note n="150"> <div sID="gen125162" type="x-p"/> “Stand in awe,” <reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.4.4">Psalm 4:4</reference>. (English Version)<div eID="gen125162" type="x-p"/> </note> The Hebrew verb <foreign xml:lang="he">רגז</foreign> (<hi type="italic">ragaz</hi>) signifies either to be agitated by anger, or, to tremble. As to the passage of the Psalm, the idea of <hi type="italic">trembling</hi> will be quite appropriate. “Do not choose to resemble madmen, who rush fearlessly in any direction, but let the dread of being accounted foolhardy keep you in awe.” The word sometimes signifies to <hi type="italic">strive</hi> or <hi type="italic">quarrel</hi>, as, in that instance, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Gen.45.24">Genesis 45:24</reference>,) “See that ye <hi type="italic">fall not out</hi> by the way;” and accordingly, the Psalmist adds, “Commune with your own heart, and be still,” — abstain from furious encounters.<div eID="gen125161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen125163" type="x-p"/>In my opinion, Paul merely alludes to the passage with the following view. There are three faults by which we offend God in being angry. The first is, when our anger arises from slight causes, and often from no cause whatever, or at least from private injuries or offenses. The second is, when we go beyond the proper bounds, and are hurried into intemperate excesses. The third is, when our anger, which ought to have been directed against ourselves or against sins, is turned against our brethren. Most appropriately, therefore, did Paul, when he wished to describe the proper limitation of anger, employ the well-known passage<hi type="italic">, Be ye angry, and sin not. </hi>We comply with this injunction, if the objects of our anger are sought, not in others, but in ourselves, — if we pour out our indignation against our own faults. With respect to others, we ought to be angry, not at their persons, but at their faults; nor ought we to be excited to anger by private offenses, but by zeal for the glory of the Lord. Lastly, our anger, after a reasonable time, ought to be allowed to subside, without mixing itself with the violence of carnal passions.<div eID="gen125163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen125164" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Let not the sun go down.</hi> It is scarcely possible, however, but that we shall sometimes give way to improper and sinful passion, — so strong is the tendency of the human mind to what is evil. Paul therefore suggests a second remedy, that we shall quickly suppress our anger, and not suffer it to gather strength by continuance. The first remedy was, <hi type="italic">Be ye angry, and sin not;</hi> but, as the great weakness of human nature renders this exceedingly difficult, the next is — not to cherish wrath too long in our minds, or allow it sufficient time to become strong. He enjoins accordingly, <hi type="italic">let not the sun go down upon your wrath.</hi> If at any time we happen to be angry, let us endeavor to be appeased before the sun has set.<div eID="gen125164" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Eph.4.26" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen125160" osisID="Eph.4.26" type="section"/>
entries.550d4767077d7ddd3b7af3052a6f3d2adf3253fa: <div annotateRef="Bible:Eph.4.27" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Eph.4.27" sID="gen125165" type="section"/> <div sID="gen125166" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">27.</hi> <hi type="italic">Neither give place</hi> (τῷ διαβόλῳ) <hi type="italic">to the devil.</hi> I am aware of the interpretation which some give of this passage. Erasmus, who translates it, “neither give place to the Slanderer,” (<foreign xml:lang="la"><hi type="italic">calumniatori</hi></foreign><hi type="italic">,</hi>) shews plainly that he understood it as referring to malicious men. But I have no doubt, Paul’s intention was, to guard us against allowing Satan to take possession of our minds, and, by keeping in his hands this citadel, to do whatever he pleases. We feel every day how impossible, or, at least, how difficult it is to cure long-continued hatred. What is the cause of this, but that, instead of resisting the devil, we yield up to him the possession of our heart? Before the poison of hatred has found its way into the heart, anger must be thoroughly dislodged.<div eID="gen125166" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Eph.4.27" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen125165" osisID="Eph.4.27" type="section"/>
entries.453f4c5acf9cb185410338f8b2527209f97b376f:
28. Let him that stole steal no more. This includes not merely the grosser thefts which are punished by human laws, but those of a more concealed nature, which do not fall under the cognizance of men, — every kind of depredation by which we seize the property of others. But he does not simply forbid us to take that property in an unjust or unlawful manner. He enjoins us to assist our brethren, as far as lies in our power.
That he may have to give to him that needeth. “Thou who formerly stolest must not only obtain thy subsistence by lawful and harmless toil, but must give assistance to others.” He is first required to labor, working with his hands, that he may not supply his wants at the expense of his brethren, but may support life by honorable labor. But the love which we owe to our neighbor carries us much farther. No one must live to himself alone, and neglect others. All must labor to supply each other’s necessities.
But a question arises, does Paul oblige all men to labor with their hands? This would be excessively hard. I reply, the meaning is plain, if it be duly considered. Every man is forbidden to steal. But many people are in the habit of pleading want, and that excuse is obviated by enjoining them rather to labor (μᾶλλον δε κοπιάτω) with their hands. As if he had said, “No condition, however hard or disagreeable, can entitle any man to do injury to another, or even to refrain from contributing to the necessities of his brethren.
The thing which is good. This latter clause, which contains an argument from the greater to the less, gives no small additional strength to the exhortation. As there are many occupations which do little to promote the lawful enjoyments of men, he recommends to them to choose those employments which yield the greatest advantage to their neighbors. We need not wonder at this. If those trades which can have no other effect than to lead men into immorality, were denounced by heathens — and Cicero among the number — as highly disgraceful, would an apostle of Christ reckon them among the lawful callings of God?
Ephesians 4:29-31
29. Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers.
29. Omnis sermo spurcus ex ore vestro non procedat; sed si quis est bonus ad edificationem usus, ut det gratiam audientibus.
30. And grieve not the Holy Spirit of God, whereby ye are sealed unto the day of redemption.
30. Et ne contristetis Spiritum Sanctum Dei, quo obsignati estis in diem redemptionis.
31. Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamor, and evil-speaking, be put away from you, with all malice.
31. Omnis amarulentia, et indignatio, et ira, et clamor, et maledicentia, removeatur a vobis cum omni malitia.
entries.5a30cd6745eff243ee6245b6fd5d7335140533b8: <div annotateRef="Bible:Eph.4.29" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Eph.4.29" sID="gen125181" type="section"/> <div sID="gen125182" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">29.</hi> <hi type="italic">No filthy speech.</hi> He first forbids believers to use any <hi type="italic">filthy</hi> language, including under this name all those expressions which are wont to be employed for the purpose of inflaming lust. Not satisfied with the removal of the vice, he enjoins them to frame their discourse for edification. In another Epistle he says, “Let your speech be seasoned with salt.” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Col.4.6">Colossians 4:6</reference>.) Here a different phrase is employed, <hi type="italic">if any</hi> (speech) <hi type="italic">be good to the use of edifying,</hi> which means simply, <hi type="italic">if it be useful.</hi> The genitive, <hi type="italic">of use,</hi> may no doubt be viewed, according to the Hebrew idiom, as put for an adjective, so that <hi type="italic">for the edification of use</hi> (πρὸς οἰκοδομὴν τὢς χρείας) may mean <hi type="italic">for useful edification;</hi> but when I consider how frequently, and in how extensive a meaning, the metaphor of <hi type="italic">edifying</hi> occurs in Paul’s writings, I prefer the former exposition. <hi type="italic">The edification of use</hi> will thus mean the progress of our edification, for to edify is to carry forward. To explain the manner in which this is done, he adds, <hi type="italic">that it may impart grace to the hearers,</hi> meaning by the word <hi type="italic">grace,</hi> comfort, advice, and everything that aids the salvation of the soul.<div eID="gen125182" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Eph.4.29" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen125181" osisID="Eph.4.29" type="section"/>
entries.00e953e90f2404a34f33bad6504e8399246a1999: <div annotateRef="Bible:Eph.4.30" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Eph.4.30" sID="gen125183" type="section"/> <div sID="gen125184" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">30.</hi> <hi type="italic">And grieve not.</hi> As the Holy Spirit dwells in us, to him every part of our soul and of our body ought to be devoted. But if we give ourselves up to aught that is impure, we may be said to drive him away from making his abode with us; and, to express this still more familiarly, human affections, such as joy and grief, are ascribed to the Holy Spirit. <note n="151"> <div sID="gen125185" type="x-p"/> “According to our view, the verse is a summation of the argument — the climax of appeal. If Christians shall persist in falsehood and deviation from the truth — if they shall indulge in fitful rage, or cherish sullen and malignant dislikes — if they shall be characterized by dishonesty, or insipid and corrupt language, then do they grieve the Holy Spirit of God; for all this perverse insubordination is in utter antagonism to the essence and operations of Him who is the Spirit of truth; and inspires the love of it; who assumed, as a fitting symbol, the form of a dove, and creates meekness and forbearance; and who, as the Spirit of holiness, leads to the appreciation of all that is just in action, noble in sentiment, and healthful and edifying in speech.” — Eadie.<div eID="gen125185" type="x-p"/> </note> Endeavour that the Holy Spirit may dwell cheerfully with you, as in a pleasant and joyful dwelling, and give him no occasion for grief. Some take a different view of it, that we grieve the Holy Spirit in others, when we offend by filthy language, or, in any other way, godly brethren, who are led by the Spirit of God. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.8.14">Romans 8:14</reference>.) Whatever is contrary to godliness is not only disrelished by godly ears, but is no sooner heard than it produces in them deep grief and pain. But that Paul’s meaning was different appears from what follows.<div eID="gen125184" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen125186" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">By whom ye are sealed.</hi> As God has sealed us by his Spirit, we grieve him when we do not follow his guidance, but pollute ourselves by wicked passions. No language can adequately express this solemn truth, that the Holy Spirit rejoices and is glad on our account, when we are obedient to him in all things, and neither think nor speak anything, but what is pure and holy; and, on the other hand, is grieved, when we admit anything into our minds that is unworthy of our calling. Now, let any man reflect what shocking wickedness there must be in grieving the Holy Spirit to such a degree as to compel him to withdraw from us. The same mode of speaking is used by the prophet Isaiah, but in a different sense; for he merely says, that they “vexed his Holy Spirit,” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.63.10">Isaiah 63:10</reference>.) in the same sense in which we are accustomed to speak of vexing the mind of a man. <hi type="italic">By whom ye are sealed.</hi> The Spirit of God is the seal, by which we are distinguished from the wicked, and which is impressed on our hearts as a sure evidence of adoption.<div eID="gen125186" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen125187" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Unto the day of redemption,</hi> — that is, till God conduct us into the possession of the promised inheritance. That day is usually called <hi type="italic">the day of redemption,</hi> because we shall then be at length delivered out of all our afflictions. It is unnecessary to make any observations on this phrase, in addition to what have already been made in expounding <reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.8.23">Romans 8:23</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Bible:1Cor.1.30">1 Corinthians 1:30</reference>. In this passage, the word <hi type="italic">sealed</hi> may have a different meaning from that which it usually bears, — that God has impressed his Spirit as his mark upon us, that he may recognize as his children those whom he perceives to bear that mark.<div eID="gen125187" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Eph.4.30" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen125183" osisID="Eph.4.30" type="section"/>
entries.8626ec5f16853b3133ab24b2b82e0aec3dbcc412:
31. Let all bitterness. He again condemns anger; but, on the present occasion, views in connection with it those offenses by which it is usually accompanied, such as noisy disputes and reproaches. Between wrath and anger (Θυμὸν καὶ ὀργὴν) there is little difference, except that the former denotes the power, and the latter the act; but here, the only difference is, that anger is a more sudden attack. The correction of all the rest will be greatly aided by the removal of malice. By this term he expresses that depravity of mind which is opposed to humanity and justice, and which is usually called malignity.
Ephesians 4:32
32. And be ye kind one to another, tender-hearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ’s sake hath forgiven you.
32. Sitis autem mutuo comes, misericordes, condonantes vobis inter vos, quemadmodum et Deus vobis in Christo condonavit.
entries.620de0a2ff0e39e11f101993e43ce1ba8de91084:
32. And be ye kind one to another. With bitterness he contrasts kindness, or gentleness of countenance, language, and manners. And as this virtue will never reign in us, unless attended by compassion, (ουμπάθεια,) he recommends to us to be tender-hearted This will lead us not only to sympathize with the distresses of our brethren, as if they were our own, but to cultivate that true humanity which is affected by everything that happens to them, in the same manner as if we were in their situation. The contrary of this is the cruelty of those iron-hearted, barbarous men, by whom the sufferings of others are beheld without any concern whatever.
Forgiving one another. The Greek word here rendered forgiving, (χαριζόμενοι ἑαυτοῖς,) is supposed by to mean beneficence. Erasmus, accordingly, renders it (largientes) bountiful. Though the word admits of that meaning, yet the context induces me to prefer the other view, that we should be ready to forgive It may sometimes happen, that men are kind and tender-hearted, and yet, when they receive improper treatment, do not so easily forgive injuries. That those whose kindness of heart in other respects disposes them to acts of humanity, may not fail in their duty through the ingratitude of men, he exhorts them to discover a readiness to lay aside resentment. To give his exhortation the greater weight, he holds out the example of God, who has forgiven to us, through Christ, far more than any mortal man can forgive to his brethren.
See Calvin's Commentary on Philippians, Colossians, etc., page 213.
CHAPTER 5
Ephesians 5:1-2
1. Be ye therefore followers of God, as dear children;
1. Sitis ergo imitatores Dei quemadmodum filii dilecti;
2. And walk in love, as Christ also hath loved us, and hath given himself for us an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweet smelling savor.
2. Et ambulate in charitate quemadmodum et Christus nos dilexit, ac se ipsum tradidit pro nobis oblationem et hostiam Deo, in odorem bonae fragrantiae.

A vertue pecu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />liar to Christians, unknown to Philosophers, see <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 20.19. <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 3.12, 13.</ns0:note> and meekness <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Whereby we are not easily provoked; or offended with the infirmities of others: this is opposed to peevishness as the former to pride.</ns0:note>, with long-suffering <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Whereby we bear with greater or repeated injuries, 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 6.6.</ns0:note>, forbearing one another <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Or <ns0:hi>supporting, i. e.</ns0:hi> bearing with the infirmities, frowardness, or moroseness of others, so as not to cease to love them, and doe them good.</ns0:note> in love <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Not out of any carnal affection, or for our own advantage, but out of Love, which is wont to make men patient and long-suffering, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 13.4.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

               <ns0:p n="4">4 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 12.5. Chap. 2.16.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:hi>There is</ns0:hi> one body <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> The Church of Christ, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 1.23. see <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 3.15.</ns0:note>, and <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">1 Cor. 12.4.</ns0:note> one Spirit <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">The self-same Spirit of Christ in that Body by which all the Members live and act, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 12.11, 13.</ns0:note> e<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ven as ye are called in one hope <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">One Inhe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ritance in Heaven, to the hope of which ye are called, <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 1.12. <ns0:hi>Hope</ns0:hi> for the thing hoped for, as <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 1.5. see 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 1 3, 4.</ns0:note> of your calling.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="5">5 <ns0:note place="margin">1 Cor. 12.5.</ns0:note> One Lord <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Christ, <ns0:hi>viz</ns0:hi> as Redeemer, Head and Husband of the Church, to whom by God's appointment she is immediately Subject, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 8.6. <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 13.13. <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 2.36.</ns0:note>, one faith <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> One object of the Faith of all Believers, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> the Doctrine of Salvation, which is but one.</ns0:note>, one baptism <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Both as to the outward Sym<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bol, and the thing signified by it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="6">6 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mal. 2.10. 1 Cor. 12.6.</ns0:note> One God <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">God is here taken Personally for the Father, the other two Persons being before mentioned, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 4.5.</ns0:note> and Father of all <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Of all Believers.</ns0:note>, who <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> above all <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Not onely in the excellencies of his Nature, but especially in his Sovereign Dominion over the Church.</ns0:note>, and through all <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">By his special Providence through all the Members of the Church.</ns0:note>, and in you all <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">By Inhabitation, and the conjunction of Belie<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vers with him. Though the former two may be applied to God's universal Dominion and Providence over all the Crea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tures, yet the Apostle speaking of the conjunction of Belie<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vers in one Father, they are both to be restrained according to this last Clause.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="7">7 But unto every one of us is given grace <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Either by Grace he means Gifts which are not common to all Believers, but proper to some, according to their va<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rious functions and places in the Church, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 12.6. 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 12.11. Or rather more generally it comprehends also those Graces which are common to all Believers as such, Faith, Hope, Love, Zeal, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> which though they are of the same kind in all, and have the same object, yet they are received in different degrees and measures.</ns0:note> according to the measure of the gift of Christ <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">In that measure in which it pleaseth Christ to give them, who gives to some one gift, to some another; to some one degree of Grace, to some another: all have not the same, but need the help of those that have what they want.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="8">8 Wherefore he <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">The Psalmist.</ns0:note> saith, When he <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Christ, God manifested in the Flesh and then what was spoken by the Psalmist Prophetically in the second Person, is spoken by the Apostle Historically in the third.</ns0:note> ascended up on high <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Christ ascended up on high after his Death, both as to place, in his humane nature, into Heaven; and chiefly as to his state in his being glorified.</ns0:note>, he led <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Or, <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 span">
                        <ns0:desc>〈…〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> captivity captive <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Either led those cap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tive who had taken us captive, or rather led them captive, whom he had taken captive; captivity being here put for captives, as elsewhere <ns0:hi>poverty</ns0:hi> for <ns0:hi>poor,</ns0:hi> 2 King. 24.14. This Christ did when having conquered sin, death, Satan, he tri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />umphed gloriously over them in his ascension, <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 2.15. it is spoken with allusion to conquering Princes or Generals, who in their Triumphs had their Captives attending upon their Chariots.</ns0:note>, and gave gifts unto men <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">He alludes in this likewise to the custome of Conquerours casting Money among the people that were the Spectatours of their Triumphs, or gave largesses to their Soul<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />diers. Christ upon his Ascension sent the Holy Ghost on the Disciples, <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 2. and continues ever since, to furnish his Church with Gifts and Graces, see on <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 68.18.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:488" />9 (Now that he ascended, what is it but that he also descended <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">The Apostle interprets the Psalmist, and concludes, that <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> when he foretold Christ's Glorification, or Ascending up to Heaven, did likewise foresee his humiliation and des<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cent to the earth, <ns0:hi>q. d.</ns0:hi> when <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> speaks of God in the Flesh ascending up on high, he doth thereby imply, that he should first descend to the Earth.</ns0:note> first into the lower parts of the earth? <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Either simply the Earth as the lowest part of the visible World, and so opposed to Heaven from whence he came down, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 3.13. and 6.33.38, 41, 42, 50, 51. or the Grave and state of the Dead; or both ra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther, implying the whole of his Humiliation in opposition to his Ascending, taken for the whole of his Exaltation.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">10 He that descended is the same that ascen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ded up <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">He saith not, he that ascended is the same that descen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ded, lest it should be thought that Christ brought his Body with him from Heaven, but on the contrary, <ns0:hi>he that des<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cended is the same that ascended,</ns0:hi> to shew that the Son of God did not by his descent become other than what he was, nor the assumption of the Humane nature add any thing to his person, as a Man is not made another person by the cloaths he puts on. Christ Descended without change of place as being God, but Ascended by changing place as Man, yet by communication of properties, whole Christ is said to have Ascended.</ns0:note> far above all heavens <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">All visible Heavens, into the third Hea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ven or Paradise, <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 3.21. <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 9.24.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note place="margin">Act. 2.33.</ns0:note> that he might <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>fulfill.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> fill all things <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">All the Members of his Church with Gifts and Graces. This began to be ful<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />filled<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                     <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 2. and still will be fulfilling to the end of the World, see <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 7.39. and 16.7.</ns0:note>)</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">11 <ns0:note place="margin">2 Tim. 4.5.</ns0:note> And he gave <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Distributed several gifts (which are spoken of in gene<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ral, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 7.) according to his Father's appointment, who is said to set in the Church what Christ is here said to give, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 12.28. <ns0:hi>Obj.</ns0:hi> Nothing is here said of Gifts, but onely of Offices. <ns0:hi>Ans.</ns0:hi> Christ never gave Offices without suitable furniture: this diversity therefore of Offices includes diver<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sity of respective Gifts.</ns0:note> some, apostles <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Extraordinary Officers with an immediate Call, universal Commission, infallibility in Teach<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing, and power of working Miracles, appointed for the first founding the Christian Church in all parts of the World, <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 28.19. <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 19.6. <ns0:hi>Obj.</ns0:hi> The Apostles were appoin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ted by Christ before his Death. <ns0:hi>Ans.</ns0:hi> The Apostle here speaks not of Christ's first calling them, but, 1. of his fully supplying them with gifts necessary to the discharge of their Office, which was after his Resurrection, <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 1.4. <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 7.39. & 2. Of their solemn Inauguration in their Office, by the pouring out of the Holy Ghost upon them in a visible manner, <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 2.</ns0:note>; and some, prophets <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Extraordinary Officers who did by im<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mediate Revelation Interpret the Scriptures, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 1.4, 5. and not onely such as did foretell things to come, <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 11.27. & 21.10.</ns0:note>; and some, evangelists <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">These were likewise extraordinary Officers for the most part chosen by the Apostles as the companions and assis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tents in Preaching the Word, and planting Churches in the se<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />veral places where they Travelled. Such were <ns0:hi>Timothy, Titus, Apollos, Silus,</ns0:hi> &c.</ns0:note>; and some, pastours and <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. 12.7.</ns0:note> teachers <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Either two names of the same Office implying the distant duties of Ruling and Teaching belong<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing to it, or two distinct Offices but both ordinary, and of standing use in the Church in all times; and then Pastours are they that are fixed to, and preside over particular Church<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />es, with the care both of instructing and ruling them, 1 <ns0:hi>Thess.</ns0:hi> 5.12. <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 13.17. called elsewhere Elders, and Bi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />shops, <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 20.28. <ns0:hi>Phil.</ns0:hi> 1.1. and 1 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 3.1. <ns0:hi>Tit.</ns0:hi> 1.5, 7. and 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 5.1, 2. Teachers, they whose work is to teach the Doctrine of Religion, and confute the contrary Errours.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">12 For the perfecting of the saints <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Either for the restoring, and bringing them into right order, who had been as it were, dissipated, and disjointed by sin, or rather the knitting together and compacting them more and more both in nearer union to Christ their Head by Faith, and to their Fellow-members by Love, see 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 1.10.</ns0:note>, for the work of the ministry <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Or for the work of <ns0:hi>Dispensation, i. e.</ns0:hi> for dispensing the Word, and all those Ordinances which it appertains to them to dispense, and so it implies their whole work. But there may be a Trajection in the words, and then this Clause is to be read before the former, and the meaning plainly is, <ns0:hi>for the work of the ministry,</ns0:hi> which is to perfect the Saints, and Edifie the Body of Christ.</ns0:note>, for the edifying of the <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 1.23. Co<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. 1.24.</ns0:note> body of Christ <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">The same in effect as perfecting the Saints, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> the building up the Church both in bringing in new members to it, and strengthning those that are brought in already, in Faith, and Holiness.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">13 Till we all come <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Or <ns0:hi>meet</ns0:hi>; All we Believers both <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Gentiles</ns0:hi> (who while in the World not onely are dispersed in several places, but have our several degrees of light and knowledge) <ns0:hi>meet,</ns0:hi> or come together in the unity of, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>into the unity.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> in the unity of the faith <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Either that perfect unity whereof Faith is the bond, or rather that perfect uni<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />formity of Faith in which we shall all have the same thoughts and apprehensions of Spiritual things<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> to which as yet, by reason of our remaining darkness we are not arrived.</ns0:note>, and of the knowledge <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Or <ns0:hi>Ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />knowledgment, i. e.</ns0:hi> not a bare speculative knowledge, but such as is joined with appropriation, and affection.</ns0:note> of the Son of God, unto a perfect man <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">He compares the mystical Body of Christ to a Man who hath his several ages and degrees of growth and strength, till he come to the height of both, and then he is a perfect Man, or a <ns0:hi>Man</ns0:hi> simply in opposition to a <ns0:hi>Child,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 13.11. The Church of Christ (expressed by a Man in the singular Number to shew its unity) hath its Infancy, its Childhood, its Youth, and is to have hereafter its perfect Manhood and state of Consistency in the other Life, when being arrived to its full pitch, it shall be past growing.</ns0:note>, unto the measure of the <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>age.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> stature of the fulness of Christ <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Either <ns0:hi>actively,</ns0:hi> that measure of stature or age which Christ fills up in it, or hath allotted to it, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 7. or rather <ns0:hi>passively,</ns0:hi> that measure which though it do not equal, yet it shall resemble, being perfectly conformed to the fulness of Christ. As in the 12. <ns0:hi>verse,</ns0:hi> he shewed the end of Christ's appointing Officers in his Church, so here he shews how long they are to continue, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> till their work be done, the Saints perfected, which will not be till they all come to the unity of the Faith, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="14">14 That we henceforth be no more <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Isa. 28.9.</ns0:note> children <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Weak in the Faith, unstable in Judgment, Chil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dren in Understanding, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 14.20. Such as need teach<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing, and strengthning, see <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 2.20. 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 3.1. <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 5.13.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. 13.9.</ns0:note> tossed to and fro <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Light and unconstant like Ships without ballast, tossed with every wave.</ns0:note>, and carried about with eve<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry wind of doctrine <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Not onely shaken and staggering as to our Faith, (as in the former Clause) but carried about to errours for want of judgment, by false Doctrines, here compared to violent Winds.</ns0:note>, by the sleight <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Their Sophistry whereby they easily Seduce those that are unskilfull, as Men easily cheat Children in playing at Dice, from whence this Meta<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phor is taken.</ns0:note> of men, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> cunning craftiness <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Their skilfulness in finding out ways of deceiving, whereby they can make any thing of any thing.</ns0:note>, whereby they lie in wait <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Viz.</ns0:hi> as in Ambush, the word here used, is translated <ns0:hi>Wiles, ch.</ns0:hi> 6.11. against which the Apostle would have them fenced with the whole armour of God, and seems to signifie a lay<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing an Ambush, or Assaulting a Man behind his Back; a secret and unseen way of circumventing, a laying wait to draw them that are Weak from the Truth.</ns0:note> to deceive.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">15 But <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Zech. 8.16.</ns0:note> speaking the <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>being sincere in love.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> truth in love <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Or <ns0:hi>following the truth</ns0:hi> in love, <ns0:hi>q. d.</ns0:hi> not onely let us not be Seduced by the craftiness of Men, but constantly adhere to, and persevere in the Belief of the Truth, joining Love with it, in which two the sum of Christianity consists; and this will be a means of our growing up, and being no more Children.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Chap. 1.22. & 2.21.</ns0:note> may grow up <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">This is opposed to being Children: we are not to stand at a stay, but grow to maturity, <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 6.1.</ns0:note> into him <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">In Knowledge, Faith, Love, and all the parts of the New Man.</ns0:note>, in all things, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Col. 1.18.</ns0:note> which is the head, <ns0:hi>even</ns0:hi> Christ <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Our growth must be with respect to Christ our Head, as the end of it; we must grow in our acknowledg<ns0:g ref="char:EOLunhyphen" />ment of him, and dependance on him, as he by whom we are influenced, and from whom all our proficiency and strength proceeds; so that whatever encrease we make, must tend not to the magnifying our selves, but exalting our Head.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="16">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:489" />16 From whom <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Christ the Head, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 15.</ns0:note> the whole body <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">The mystical Body, or Church of Believers, whereof every true Saint is a Member, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 12.4, 5.</ns0:note> fitly join<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed together <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Viz.</ns0:hi> in the right place and order, both in respect of Christ the Head, and of the Members respectively. Some are eyes, some ears, some hands, some feet, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 12.15, 16.</ns0:note>, and compacted <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Firmly knit, so as not to be separated.</ns0:note> by that which every joint supplieth <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Or by every joint, or juncture of <ns0:hi>Administration, i. e.</ns0:hi> whose Office is to administer Spirits, and nourishment to the Body. <ns0:hi>Bands</ns0:hi> are added to joints, <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 2.19. which signifies the Liga<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ments by which the joints are tied one to another, aswell as the joints in which they touch. <ns0:hi>Qu.</ns0:hi> What are those joints and bands in the mystical Body? <ns0:hi>Ans.</ns0:hi> Every thing whereby Believers are joined to Christ, or to each other as Christians; especially the Spirit of Christ, which is the same in the Head, and all the Members: the gifts of the Spirit, chiefly Faith, whereby they are united to Christ; and Love, whereby they are knit to each other: the Sacraments likewise, Church Officers, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 11. <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, according to the effectual working <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Either the Power of Christ, who as an Head, influenceth and enliveneth every Member; or the effectual working of every Member, in communicating to others the gifts it hath recei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ved.</ns0:note> in the measure of every part <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">According to the state, condition, and exigency of every part, nourishment is conveyed to it meet for it; yet more to one, and less to another, according as more is re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quired for one and less for the other, and so to all in their proportion. Or else as each part hath received, so it com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />municates to others: all have their use and helpfulness to others, but not all alike, or in the same degree.</ns0:note>, maketh encrease of the body <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Either <ns0:hi>Body</ns0:hi> here redounds by an <ns0:hi>Hebraism,</ns0:hi> and the sense is, the Body (mentioned in the beginning of the verse) maketh encrease of it self, or without that redundancy, encrease of the Body is an encrease meet and convenient for the Body. The Apostle here changeth the Metaphor from that of a Bo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dy to this of an House, but to the same sense, and shews the end of this nourishment they ministred from one Member to another, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> not its own private good, but the good of the whole Body, for the benefit of which each part receives its gifts from Christ the Head.</ns0:note>, unto the edifying of it self in love <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Either by the Offices of love; or it denotes the impulsive cause, whereby the members are moved thus to promote the common increase of the body, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> Love to the Head and each other.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="17">17 This I say therefore and testifie in the Lord <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">I beseech or adjure you by the Lord, see the like, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 12.1. <ns0:hi>Phil.</ns0:hi> 2.1.</ns0:note>, that ye <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Pet. 4.3.</ns0:note> henceforth walk not as other Gentiles walk <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Rom. 1.21.</ns0:note> in the vanity of their mind <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Their minds themselves, and understan<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dings, the highest and noblest faculties in them, being con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />versant about things empty, transient, and unprofitable, and which deceive their expectations, and therefore vain, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> their Idols, their Worldly enjoyments, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="18">18 Having the understanding <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">The mind as reasoning and discoursing, and so their ratiocinations, and discourses themselves.</ns0:note> darkned <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">As to Spiritual things.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 2.12.</ns0:note> being alienated <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Not onely strangers to it, (for so are those Crea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tures which are not capable of it) but estranged from it; implying, that in <ns0:hi>Adam</ns0:hi> originally they were not so.</ns0:note> from the life of God <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">A Spiritual life; that life which God commands, and approves, and whereby God lives in Believers, and they live in him, <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 2.19, 20. and that both as to the principle of life, and the operations of it.</ns0:note>, through the ignorance that is in them <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">That ignorance which is naturally in them is the cause of their alienation from the Life of God, which begins in light, and knowledge.</ns0:note>, because of the <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Rom. 1.24.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>hardness of their hearts.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> blindness of their heart <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Or rather <ns0:hi>hard<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness</ns0:hi>: the <ns0:hi>Gr.</ns0:hi> word signifies a <ns0:hi>cal<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="3 letters">

Either this is set down as another cause of their estrangement from the Life of God, or as the cause of their ignorance, which though in part it be natural to them, yet is encreased to far<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther degrees by their own hardness and obstinacy, shutting their eyes voluntarily against the light.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="19">19 Who being past feeling <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Having lost all sense and conscience of Sin.                <ns0:p n="20">20 But ye have not so <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">So as to walk as other <ns0:hi>Gentiles</ns0:hi> walk, in the vanity of your minds, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> learned Christ <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">The Doctrine of Christ, or Rule of Life prescribed by him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="21">21 If so be that ye have heard him <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Either heard Christ speaking to you in the Gospel, <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 12.25. and then the sense will be the same as in the follow<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing Clause: or heard him Preached to you, and then it may refer to the outward hearing of the word.</ns0:note>, and have been taught by him <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Or Taught <ns0:hi>in</ns0:hi> him: <ns0:hi>in</ns0:hi> for <ns0:hi>by,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 1.16. <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 1.2. and then this relates to the power of the word, and the impression made by it upon the heart, <ns0:hi>q. d.</ns0:hi> if ye have not onely heard of him by the hearing of the Ear, but have been effectually taught by the Spirit to know him, and receive his Doctrine, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 54.13. <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 6.45.</ns0:note>, as the truth is in Jesus <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">As it really is, and hath been taught by Christ himself both in his Doctrine and Example, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> What is the true way of a Christian's living, as in the following verses, see <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 17.17. <ns0:hi>Tit.</ns0:hi> 1.1.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Which draw away and entice men, <ns0:hi>Iam.</ns0:hi> 1.14. or which put on a shew and semblance of some good, or promise pleasure and happiness, but lurch mens hopes, and make them more miserable.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="23">23 And be <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 12.2.</ns0:note> renewed <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Viz.</ns0:hi> more and more, being already renewed in part</ns0:note> in the spirit of your mind <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> In your mind which is a Spirit, see 1 <ns0:hi>Thess.</ns0:hi> 5.23. and 2 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 4.22.                <ns0:p n="24">24 And that ye put <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 6.4.                      <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> A new disposition or constitution of the whole man, called the New Creature, 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 5.17. and a Divine Nature, 2 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 1.4.                   </ns0:note> true <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Sincere and Sound. As Righteousness and Holiness are opposed to <ns0:hi>lusts, v.</ns0:hi> 22. so <ns0:hi>true</ns0:hi> here, to <ns0:hi>deceitfull</ns0:hi> there.</ns0:note> holiness.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="25">25 Wherefore putting away lying <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">All fraudulency, and dissimulation and whatever is contrary to truth.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Zach. 8.16.</ns0:note> speak every man truth <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Not onely speak as things are, but act sincerely and candidly.</ns0:note> with his neighbour; for <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Rom. 12.5.</ns0:note> we are members one of another <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> To or <ns0:hi>for</ns0:hi> one another, and therefore must be helpfull to each other.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="26">26 Be <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 4.4. & 37.8.</ns0:note> ye angry <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">By way of Concession rather than by way of Command, <ns0:hi>q. d.</ns0:hi> if the case be such tha<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> ye must be angry, yet see it be without sin.</ns0:note> and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">If your anger is excessive (for so this word signifies, being different from the former) yet let it not be lasting; be reconciled e'er the Sun go down.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="27">27 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Jam. 4.7. 1 Pet. 5.9.</ns0:note> Neither give place to the Devil <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Do not give advantage to the Devil to possess your hearts, and put you upon more<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> and greater evils, see <ns0:hi>Luk.</ns0:hi> 22.3. <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 13.27. <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 5.3.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:489" />28 Let him that stole, steal no more <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Stealing is understood largely for seeking our own gain by any way defrauding others, whether by taking away, or unjustly detaining what is theirs. <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Diligently and In<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dustriously, as the word imports.                         <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> Thess. 3.8, 11, 12.</ns0:note> let him labour <ns0:hi>e,</ns0:hi> working with <ns0:hi>his</ns0:hi> hands <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">As the onely instrument by which most Arts and Trades are exercised.</ns0:note> the thing which is good <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Not in any unlaw<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />full way, but in an honest calling.</ns0:note>, that he may have <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>distri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="4 letters">
                           <ns0:desc>••••</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> to give to him that needeth <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">That he may have not onely whereupon to live, and prevent stealing, but where<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />with to help those that want, <ns0:hi>Luk.</ns0:hi> 21.2.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="29">29 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 5.4.</ns0:note> Let no corrupt communication <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Unprofitable, unsavoury, not seasoned with the salt of prudence, <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 4.6. see <ns0:hi>Mark.</ns0:hi> 9.50.</ns0:note> pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceed out of your mouth, but that which is good <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>to edifie profitably.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> to the use of edifying that <ns0:note n="⸫" place="bottom">Gr. <ns0:hi>to the edi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fication of use,</ns0:hi> by an <ns0:hi>Hypallage</ns0:hi> for, <ns0:hi>to the use of edifying,</ns0:hi> (as our Translators render it) implying, that the great use of Speech is to Edifie those with whom we converse.                      <ns0:hi>Viz.</ns0:hi> by corrupt Communication.                <ns0:p n="31">31 Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">These all seem to relate to the inward affection, as the two following to the effects of it in the words.
